## Bot Clicks on Tracking Links: Clean Your Click Data Before You Judge a Creator

URL: https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/bot-clicks-tracking-links
Language: English
Published: 2026-11-05
Author: Luke

## Why bot clicks distort creator results

A creator's link shows 300 clicks. Installs: 12. Did the audience lose interest between tap and store, or were many of those clicks never people at all?

Often it's the second. One founder who checked his numbers found that "most raw clicks turned out to be bots." We see it in our own data too: in a small batch of outreach links we sent last month, 4 of 9 raw clicks came from our own tests and automated link previews, not from the people we wrote to.

## Where non-human clicks come from

| Source | What happens | Typical sign |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Link previews | Messaging apps and social platforms fetch a link to build a preview card | A click within seconds of the link being posted or sent |
| Email security scanners | Corporate email systems open every link to check it's safe | A click soon after an email is delivered, often from a data center |
| Search and social crawlers | Bots index pages that contain your link | Regular clicks with no installs, unusual user agents |
| Monitoring and testing | Your team, your QA, uptime checks | Clicks from your office, your city or known test devices |
| Click fraud | Deliberate fake clicks to inflate results | Large bursts, odd countries, no downstream events |

Most non-human clicks aren't malicious. They're a side effect of how the internet checks and previews links. They still distort click-based reports.

  

[Bot clicks on tracking links: five sources of non-human clicks are link previews, email security scanners, search and social crawlers, monitoring and testing, and click fraud, each with a typical sign]

## Why clicks are the wrong scoreboard

Even human clicks are a weak signal for creator value. Many viewers search the App Store instead of tapping, and some who tap never install. Clicks sit at the top of the funnel, where noise is highest and value is lowest.

The numbers that matter are further down: installs, trial starts, paying subscribers and cost per subscriber. Those are much harder to fake by accident. If you pay creators on CPM, the same idea applies to views: [track cost per subscriber, not just views](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/creator-cpm-cost-per-subscriber).

## How to clean click data when you do read it

1.  **Exclude your own tests.** Tag internal test devices, or note the times you tested each link.
    
2.  **Ignore clicks within seconds of posting or sending.** These are usually previews or scanners.
    
3.  **Watch for data-center traffic.** Clicks from cloud hosting providers are rarely people browsing.
    
4.  **Check geography.** Clicks from countries the creator doesn't reach deserve a closer look.
    
5.  **Look for bursts.** Dozens of clicks in a minute with no installs is a red flag.
    
6.  **Compare click-to-install rates across creators.** A creator with far more clicks per install than everyone else needs a closer look.
    

Many attribution tools apply some of these filters automatically, but it's still worth knowing what's in your numbers.

## What to put in creator reports instead

| Metric | Why it's better than clicks |
| --- | --- |
| Installs from the link | A real device installed the app |
| Trial starts | A person showed intent to pay |
| Paying subscribers | The outcome you pay creators for |
| Cost per subscriber | Compares creators on value, not volume |

Add onboarding survey mentions to catch people who searched the store instead of tapping, so creators with "low clicks" aren't undervalued.

## Key points

-   Link previews, email security scanners, search crawlers, monitoring tools and your own tests all register as clicks.
    
-   **Don't judge creators on clicks.** Judge them on installs, trial starts and subscribers.
    
-   When you do read clicks, filter out obvious non-human traffic and your own tests first.
    

## Bot clicks FAQ

### Why do my tracking links show clicks but no installs?

Often because many clicks aren't people: link previews, email scanners, crawlers and your own tests. Some real visitors also leave the store page without installing. Judge links on installs and trials, not clicks.

### Do link previews count as clicks?

They can. When a messaging app or social platform builds a preview, it fetches the link, which many systems record as a click.

### Do email security scanners click links?

Many corporate email systems open links in incoming emails to check them, which can register as clicks shortly after delivery.

### How do I stop bots from inflating my creator link clicks?

You can't stop all of them, but you can filter tests, instant clicks, data-center traffic and bursts, and you can judge creators on installs, trials and subscribers instead.

### Is a high click-to-install gap a sign of fraud?

Not necessarily. It's more often previews and scanners. Look at timing, geography and bursts before drawing conclusions, and compare with other creators.

## Judge creators on what happens after the click

Clicks are the noisiest number in creator marketing. Clean them before you read them, and never use them to decide who to renew. Installs, trials and subscribers tell you who actually brought value.

## Paying Creators a Revenue Share: How to Track Subscription Commissions Fairly

URL: https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/creator-revenue-share-subscription-commissions
Language: English
Published: 2026-11-05
Author: Luke

## How creator revenue share works for subscription apps

Paying creators per view rewards reach. Paying them a share of subscription revenue rewards results. That's why more subscription apps are moving creators and affiliates to commissions. One app we spoke with already pays per sign-up, "so long as we believed they were legitimate users with complete profiles." Others have built their own affiliate tracking from scratch.

Revenue share sounds simple. In practice, it depends on two things: knowing which creator brought each subscriber, and writing down clear rules for what you pay.

## A quick example: 20% of what?

A $39.99 annual plan doesn't put $39.99 in your account. With a 15% store fee, you receive about $33.99, so a 20% commission on net revenue comes to about $6.80, not $8.00. Step 4 below covers how to set this up.

  

[Creator revenue share example: a $39.99 annual plan minus a 15% store fee leaves $33.99 in net revenue, and a 20% commission on net revenue is $6.80 (illustrative)]

## Step 1: Credit each subscriber to one creator

Commissions need user-level credit. Use two signals together:

-   **A tracking link per creator** in their bio or Story link sticker, which follows each person who taps through install, trial and subscription.
    
-   **A personal code per creator**, entered in onboarding, for people who saw the video and searched the store instead.
    

Decide what happens when both apply: for example, the link wins if the person tapped it within 7 days, otherwise the code. Write it down. Disputes usually come from unwritten rules.

Codes alone undercount and can leak to coupon sites, which we cover in [our post on creator promo code tracking](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/creator-promo-code-tracking).

## Step 2: Decide what earns commission

| Decision | Common options | What to consider |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Which payments | First payment only; first year; lifetime | Lifetime is generous but grows your liability |
| Which plans | All plans; annual only | Annual plans pay more up front |
| Rate | Flat fee per subscriber; % of revenue | A flat fee is simpler; % scales with price |
| Base amount | Gross price; net after store fees | Net protects your margin |
| Free trials | No commission until the first payment | Paying on trials invites low-quality traffic |

A common, simple starting point: a percentage of net revenue for the first 12 months of each subscriber, paid monthly.

## Step 3: Handle refunds and hold periods

Subscribers can request refunds, and some payments fail. Protect yourself:

-   **Hold commissions for 30 to 60 days** after each payment before paying out.
    
-   **Reverse commissions** on refunded or charged-back payments within that window.
    
-   **Pay on confirmed revenue** from your subscription platform, not on in-app events.
    

## Step 4: Calculate on net revenue

Stores take a fee on in-app purchases and subscriptions, and the rate depends on the store, your program and the plan. Calculate commissions on what you actually receive. For example, on a $39.99 annual plan with a 15% store fee, a 20% commission on net revenue is about $6.80, not $8.00.

## Step 5: Share a monthly report

Creators trust programs they can see. Each month, send each creator: link taps, installs, trials, paying subscribers, refunds, net revenue and commission earned. Transparent numbers also help creators make more of what works.

## Step 6: Watch for abuse

-   Codes appearing on coupon sites.
    
-   Spikes of subscribers from countries the creator doesn't reach.
    
-   Many subscriptions that cancel or refund right after the first payment.
    

The hold period and refund reversals handle most of it. For the rest, reserve the right to review in your creator agreement.

## Before you sign a revenue share deal

-   Credit each subscriber to one creator using a **tracking link plus a code**.
    
-   Set clear rules for **which payments earn commission, for how long, and on what amount** (net of store fees and refunds).
    
-   Hold payouts until the refund window passes.
    
-   Share a simple monthly report with each creator.
    

## Revenue share FAQ

### How do I pay creators a percentage of subscription revenue?

Credit each subscriber to one creator with a tracking link and a code, calculate commission on net revenue for the payments your rules cover, hold payouts through the refund window, and pay monthly with a report.

### Should creator commissions be on gross or net revenue?

Net revenue, after store fees and refunds, is safer for your margin and easier to defend. State it clearly in the agreement.

### How long should creators earn commission on a subscriber?

Many programs pay for the first year of each subscriber. Lifetime commissions are more generous but grow your long-term costs.

### Should I pay commission on free trials?

Usually not. Paying on trials rewards volume, not quality. Pay from the first confirmed payment.

### Can I combine a flat fee with a revenue share?

Yes. A small flat fee per video plus a revenue share is a common hybrid. It keeps creator income predictable and ties part of it to results.

## Fair for both sides

Revenue share aligns creators with what you care about: paying subscribers. Make it fair with clear attribution, written rules, net-revenue math, a hold period and an honest monthly report.

## Creator Brief Template for Apps: Make Conversions Trackable Without a Hard CTA

URL: https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/creator-brief-template-app-conversions
Language: English
Published: 2026-11-05
Author: Luke

## A creator brief template that keeps conversions trackable

Creators know their audiences don't like ads. So most keep the app mention natural. One founder who works with several creators described what that means in practice: "most creators are not doing hard CTAs. There's a link in bio for most but it doesn't drive traffic."

That isn't a creator problem. A marketer who studies creator formats put it well: "it isn't creators job to bring you customers. It's their audience but you have to provide the right brief and format for their audience to convert."

**In short**

-   Don't ask for a hard sell. Brief the small details that let viewers find you and let you count them:
    
    -   **Say and show the app name**
        
    -   **One soft call to action**
        
    -   **A link where it can be tapped**
        
    -   **A code only if it unlocks something**
        
    -   **Posting dates spaced apart**
        
    -   **Clear ad disclosure**
        
-   Measure with a link, an onboarding question and the lift after each post.
    

## A simple brief template

| Section | What to include |
| --- | --- |
| About the app | One sentence on the problem it solves, for whom |
| The moment to show | The screen or result that proves it works |
| Must-haves | Say and show the app name; one soft CTA; link in bio and Story sticker; disclosure |
| Nice-to-haves | Personal code; search hint; your favorite feature |
| Don'ts | Claims you can't support; competitor mentions; hard-sell scripts |
| Logistics | Posting date and time; link and code; deliverables; payment terms |

  

[Creator brief template for apps: about the app, the moment to show, must-haves, nice-to-haves, don'ts and logistics, with the must-haves highlighted as the parts that make results measurable]

The rest of this guide explains each must-have and why it matters for tracking.

## Why the brief decides what you can measure

Most viewers who act on a creator video don't tap a link. They remember the app and search for it later. If they can't remember the name, or spell it, they can't find you, and you can't credit the creator. A good brief makes the search path easy and leaves a trace for each path you can track.

## The trackable creator brief: a checklist

### 1\. Make the app name unmissable

-   Say the exact app name out loud at least once.
    
-   Show it on screen as text, ideally with the App Store or Google Play icon.
    
-   If the name is hard to spell or shared with other apps, add a search hint: "search \[App name\] \[category\]".
    

### 2\. One soft call to action

Ask for one natural line, not a pitch. For example: "It's called \[App name\], it's free to try," or "Link's in my bio if you want to try it." One clear next step beats three.

### 3\. Put the link where it can be tapped

Links in TikTok and Instagram captions and comments aren't clickable, and YouTube Shorts descriptions and comments don't have clickable links either. Ask for:

-   A tracking link in the creator's bio for the campaign period.
    
-   An Instagram Story with a link sticker on posting day.
    
-   For long-form YouTube, a link in the description.
    

### 4\. Use a code only if it unlocks something

A personal code helps catch people who search, but only if typing it gets them something, like a longer trial. Ask the creator to say and show it. Expect codes to undercount, as we explain in [our post on creator promo code tracking](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/creator-promo-code-tracking).

### 5\. Show the app doing its job

The best-converting creator videos usually show the app solving a real problem in the first seconds, in the creator's own words. Give creators the problem and the moment to show; let them choose the words.

### 6\. Agree on posting dates

Space creators at least three to four days apart, so you can read each post's effect separately. Get the posting date and time in writing.

### 7\. Clear disclosure

Paid creator content needs to be disclosed clearly. In the US, the FTC explains what creators should do in its guide [Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/disclosures-101-social-media-influencers). Use the platform's paid partnership label too. Clear disclosure protects you and the creator.

  

[FTC Disclosures 101 for Social Media Influencers: if you endorse a product through social media, your message should make it obvious when you have a material connection with the brand, such as being paid or getting free products]

_The FTC's Disclosures 101 guide asks creators to make any material connection with a brand obvious, such as payment or free products. Source: Federal Trade Commission_

## How to measure the result

After each post, read three signals: link installs and trials, mentions in your onboarding question ("Where did you hear about us?"), and the lift in trial starts over the next seven days. We cover how they fit together in [Creator Attribution for Apps: How to Credit Installs When Viewers Skip the Link](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/creator-attribution-app-store-search).

## Creator brief FAQ

### What should a creator brief for an app include?

The problem the app solves, the moment to show on screen, the exact app name to say and show, one soft call to action, link placement, an optional code, posting dates and disclosure rules.

### Should creators use a hard call to action for apps?

Usually not. A natural mention with the app name said and shown often works better and feels more authentic. One soft, clear next step is enough.

### Where should creators put app links?

In their bio and in an Instagram Story link sticker. Links in TikTok and Instagram captions and comments, and in YouTube Shorts descriptions and comments, aren't clickable. Long-form YouTube descriptions can carry links.

### Do creators need to disclose paid app promotions?

Yes. Paid content should be clearly disclosed. In the US, see the FTC's guidance for influencers, and use each platform's paid partnership label.

### How do I measure a creator video if few people tap the link?

Combine the link with an onboarding question and the lift in trial starts after the post, and compare creators on cost per trial and cost per subscriber.

## Copy, adapt, send

You don't need creators to sell hard. You need them to make your app easy to find and easy to count. Brief the name, one soft CTA, a tappable link, an optional code, spaced dates and clear disclosure, then measure with three signals.

Many subscription apps find their best ads by accident: an organic TikTok video takes off. The natural next step is to put money behind it. One founder described his playbook: "Whenever a video starts to go viral, we promote it with TikTok and Meta paid ads as quickly as possible."

**Quick take**

-   Pick videos to boost by **trial signal**, not views alone.
    
-   Boost them in an app campaign **optimized for trial starts**.
    
-   Measure paid results with your attribution setup and organic results with links and an onboarding question, so you can see what the boost added.
    
-   Judge the result on **cost per trial and cost per subscriber**.
    

## How Spark Ads work

According to TikTok's help center, you can use posts from:

-   **Your own or a linked TikTok account,** such as your brand account or a creator account linked through Business Center.
    
-   **A creator's video, authorized with a code.** The creator generates a video code in the TikTok app and shares it with you, and you use it to authorize the post as an ad.

A few practical notes from TikTok's guide: the caption can't be edited after the post is authorized as an ad, so finalize it first, and a private video becomes public when used in a campaign.

## Step 1: Pick winners by trial signal, not views alone

Views tell you a video spreads. They don't tell you it brings subscribers. Before boosting, check:

-   **Trial lift** in the days after the video went live, compared with your baseline.
    
-   **Link installs and trials** from the account's bio link.
    
-   **Onboarding survey mentions** of TikTok or the creator.
    

A video with fewer views but a clear trial lift is often a better boost candidate than a viral one with none. If you post from several accounts, here's [how to measure UGC formats across multiple accounts](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/ugc-format-testing-multiple-accounts) before you pick what to boost.

## Step 2: Boost with the right objective

For a subscription app, set up the boost as an app campaign optimized for an in-app event, ideally the **trial start**, rather than video views or installs. That way TikTok's system looks for people likely to start a trial. Make sure the trial start event is set up and firing once per person before you launch.

## Step 3: Keep paid and organic separate

A boosted video keeps earning organic views too, so results mix. Keep them apart:

-   **Paid results** come through your attribution setup for the TikTok campaign.
    
-   **Organic results** come through the bio link, the onboarding question and baseline lift.
    
-   **Don't double count:** a person attributed to the paid campaign shouldn't also be counted as organic.

## Step 5: Refresh before fatigue

Even great videos wear out as the same people see them again. Watch cost per trial week by week, and line up the next organic winner before the current one fades.

## Spark Ads FAQ

### What are TikTok Spark Ads?

Spark Ads are ads that use organic TikTok posts, from your own or linked accounts or from creators who authorize their videos with a code, so the ad appears as native content.

### How do I get a creator's video for Spark Ads?

Ask the creator to generate a video code in the TikTok app and share it with you, then use it in TikTok Ads Manager to authorize their post.

### Should I boost the video with the most views?

Not automatically. Boost the videos that brought the most trials organically. Views show reach, not intent.

## Why podcast and YouTube sponsorships are harder to measure

Podcasts and long-form YouTube are different from short-form video. People listen while driving, cooking or working out. They can't tap anything in that moment, and they often act days or weeks later. And a good episode keeps finding new listeners for months.

That's why sponsorships are often hard to read. One founder told us he works with "6-10 creators, affiliates, podcasts, and a YouTube," and that "attribution back to the exact creator is difficult."

## Why long-form is different

| Factor | Short-form video | Podcasts and long-form YouTube |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Can the audience tap? | Rarely, links sit in the bio | Podcasts: no, while listening; YouTube: yes, in the description |
| When do people act? | Hours to days | Days to weeks |
| How long does it keep working? | Mostly the first week | Months, as episodes keep getting played or found in search |
| What do people remember? | The app's look | What the host said |

## Step 1: Give listeners something to remember

-   **A vanity link** that's easy to say: yourapp.com/showname. It should redirect through a tracking link so visits and installs are credited to the show.
    
-   **A personal code** that unlocks something, like an extended trial, so people bother to type it. Codes undercount on their own, so see [how to track creator codes fairly](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/creator-promo-code-tracking).
    
-   **The app name, said clearly,** with how to find it: "search \[App name\] in the App Store."
    

## Step 2: Put a tappable link where it works

-   **YouTube:** a tracking link in the video description and, if the creator agrees, in a pinned comment on long-form videos. (Links in YouTube Shorts descriptions and comments [aren't clickable](https://tubefilter.com/2023/08/10/youtube-shorts-comments-spam/).)
    
-   **Podcasts:** a tracking link in the show notes on every platform where the episode is published.
    

## Step 3: Ask listeners directly

Add show names to your onboarding question during active sponsorships. Listeners are usually happy to tell you which show they heard, and many will never use a link or a code. For podcasts, this is often your biggest signal.

## Step 4: Use a long window

Read results at 7, 30 and 90 days. For each show, add up:

-   Installs, trials and subscribers from the vanity link and show-notes or description link.
    
-   Code redemptions.
    
-   Onboarding mentions.
    

Then compare with the lift in trial starts around each episode's release. Expect a peak in the first week and a long tail after.

## Step 5: Compare shows on cost per subscriber

| Show | Cost | Link trials | Code uses | Survey mentions | Est. subscribers (90 days) | Cost per subscriber |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Podcast A | $1,500 | 18 | 22 | 61 | 40 | $37.50 |
| YouTube B | $2,000 | 74 | 15 | 38 | 52 | $38.46 |
| Podcast C | $800 | 3 | 5 | 9 | 6 | $133.33 |

_Numbers are illustrative._

Podcast A looks weak on links but strong in the survey: its listeners remember the host, not the URL. Without the survey, you'd have dropped your best show.

## Takeaways

-   Give listeners an easy path they can remember: a **short, spoken vanity link** and a **personal code** that unlocks something.
    
-   Put a **tracking link in the show notes or video description**.
    
-   Ask **"Where did you hear about us?"** in onboarding, with show names listed.
    
-   Read results over a **30 to 90 day window**, not seven days.
    

## Sponsorship measurement FAQ

### How do I track app installs from a podcast ad?

Use a spoken vanity link that redirects through a tracking link, a personal code, a link in the show notes, and an onboarding question listing the show. Read results over 30 to 90 days.

### How long after a podcast or YouTube sponsorship should I measure?

At least 30 days, ideally 90. Long-form episodes keep getting listens and views for months.

### Are vanity URLs good for podcast attribution?

Yes, when they're short, easy to say, and redirect through a tracking link. They still miss people who search the store, so add a code and a survey.

### Can I put a tracking link in a YouTube description?

Yes, for long-form videos. Links in YouTube Shorts descriptions and comments aren't clickable.

### How do I compare podcasts with YouTube sponsorships?

Add up link, code and survey signals per show over the same window, estimate subscribers, and compare cost per subscriber.

## Where to start

Long-form sponsorships are heard more than they're tapped, and they keep working long after release. Give listeners a memorable path, ask them where they heard about you, and read results over months, not days.

## Ad Clicks but No Sign-Ups? Track Every Step Between Your Ad and Your App

URL: https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/ad-clicks-no-signups-funnel-tracking
Language: English
Published: 2026-11-05
Author: Luke

## Ad clicks but no sign-ups: where people drop off

One founder shared her first ad test in public: "150 clicks, a 2.1% click-through rate... Signups: zero." The ads were doing their job. People were interested enough to click. Something between the click and the sign-up was losing all of them.

When she tracked each step, the answer was clear: most of those visitors "bounced on the landing page and never reached the signup page." Another founder reached the same conclusion about his own test: "That points at my landing page, not the audience."

**What to do**

- Before you change the audience, the creative or the channel, **track every step between the ad and the sign-up**: landing page view, scroll or key interaction, store button tap, store visit, install, sign-up or trial.

- Find the **biggest drop** and fix that first.

- Clicks with no sign-ups is a funnel problem far more often than a traffic problem.

## The steps between an ad and a sign-up

For an app that sends ads to a web page first, the path usually looks like this:

| Step                            | What to track                      | Common reasons people leave                      |
|---------------------------------|------------------------------------|--------------------------------------------------|
| 1. Ad click                    | Clicks by campaign and ad          | (Not a drop yet, but check for non-human clicks) |
| 2. Landing page loads          | Page views, load time              | Slow page, especially on mobile                  |
| 3. Engagement                  | Scroll depth, taps on key elements | Headline doesn't match the ad; unclear value     |
| 4. Store or sign-up button tap | Button taps                        | Button below the fold; too many choices          |
| 5. Store page visit            | Visits by source                   | Generic store page that doesn't match the ad     |
| 6. Install                     | Installs by source                 | Store page doesn't convince                      |
| 7. Sign-up or trial start      | In-app events by source            | Long onboarding; account required too early      |

[Funnel tracking from ad click to sign-up: seven steps to track are ad click, landing page load, engagement, store or sign-up tap, store page visit, install, and sign-up or trial start]

## Step 1: Make sure the clicks are real

Some clicks come from link previews, crawlers and your own tests. Check that clicks turn into landing page views at a sensible rate. If many clicks never load the page, the problem may be the data, not the funnel.

## Step 2: Tag every step

- Carry campaign parameters from the ad to the landing page.

- Track page views, scroll depth and taps on your main buttons.

- Use a tracking link on the store button, so installs are credited to the page and the campaign that sent the visitor.

- Track sign-up and trial start in the app, tied to the same source.

## Step 3: Find the biggest drop

Here's how the founder's funnel looked once she tracked each step, in her own numbers:

- She moved the ad to a new page with a sample plan visitors could explore.

- "64 people landed on the sample plan, 58% scrolled or tapped, and 14% opened the inputs. Of those that opened the inputs, 33% went on to run their own numbers."

- Her conclusion: "getting people from looking to actually opening the inputs is the step I'm working on."

That's the whole method: see each step's rate, find the step with the biggest drop, and work on that one.

## Step 4: Fix the most common leaks

- **Match the ad and the page.** The page's headline should repeat the promise in the ad.

- **Make the page fast on mobile.** Most ad clicks come from phones.

- **Show the value before asking for anything.** Let people see an example or result first.

- **One clear next step.** A single "Get the app" or "Start free trial" button, visible without scrolling.

- **Send people to the right store page.** Use a link that opens the App Store or Google Play based on the device, and keep the store page consistent with the ad.

- **Shorten onboarding.** Ask for an account only when it's needed.

## Step 5: Judge the channel after the funnel works

Once each step converts at a healthy rate, compare channels on cost per sign-up, cost per trial and cost per subscriber. Judging a channel through a leaky funnel tells you about your funnel, not about the channel.

## Funnel tracking FAQ

### Why do my ads get clicks but no sign-ups?

Usually because people drop off between the click and the sign-up: a slow or unclear landing page, a button that's hard to find, a store page that doesn't match the ad, or a long onboarding. Track each step to find where.

### How do I track the funnel from ad click to app install?

Carry campaign parameters to your landing page, track page views and button taps, use a tracking link on your store button, and track sign-ups and trials in the app tied to the same source.

### Should I send ad traffic to a landing page or directly to the App Store?

Test both. A landing page lets you explain more and capture people who aren't ready to install; direct store traffic has fewer steps. Compare on cost per trial and cost per subscriber.

### What's a good click-to-install rate?

It varies widely by channel, audience and app. Watch your own rate over time and compare campaigns, rather than chasing a universal benchmark.

### Could the clicks be fake?

Some may be link previews, crawlers or tests. Check that clicks turn into page views before you diagnose the funnel.

## Fix the biggest drop first

Clicks with no sign-ups is a gift: people are interested, and something fixable is in the way. Track every step, find the biggest drop, fix it, and only then judge the channel.

### Can I add an attribution SDK to a Kids Category app?

Maybe. Apple's rules limit third-party analytics there, and the answer depends on your app and the SDK. Read the current guidelines, get counsel's view, and ask the vendor exactly what the SDK collects.

### Do I need attribution if Apple Ads is my only paid channel?

Possibly not. Apple's own reports may answer your questions for a while. Attribution earns its cost when you add a second channel, or when you want trial and subscription results in one view with your other traffic.

## App Store Keyword Research for Subscription Apps

URL: https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/app-store-keyword-research-subscription-apps
Language: English
Published: 2026-11-05
Author: Hyunjong Choi

App Store keyword research looks like a data problem. In practice, most of the data is an estimate, and the people who use it most admit that. So you need a method that holds up when the numbers are soft.

This method comes from App Masters, the App Store Optimization (ASO) agency and YouTube channel founded by Steve P. Young, checked against Apple's documentation. App Masters sells ASO services, some of its videos are sponsored, and its results are its own reported wins. So we separate what Apple documents, what App Masters reports and what we think. Scores such as 30 are starting points. This guide covers iOS.

## What Apple documents, and what it doesn't

Start with the facts, because they set the limits of everything else.

Apple says search results depend on text relevance and user behavior. Text relevance means matches in your app name, subtitle, keywords and primary category. User behavior includes downloads, ratings and reviews.

Apple also sets these rules:

- Your app name and subtitle can each run to 30 characters.
- The keyword field holds 100 characters, separated by commas with no spaces.
- Don't repeat words already in your name, subtitle or category. A plural of a word you already use counts as a duplicate.
- Don't use competing app names in keywords. Guideline 2.3.7 also warns against packing metadata with trademarked terms, popular app names or irrelevant phrases.
- Keywords should describe your app accurately.
- Promotional text does not affect search ranking.

Apple does not publish how much each field weighs, and it does not say that a keyword in the app name beats one in the keyword field. App Masters' view is that the app name carries the most weight, then the subtitle, then the keyword field.

## Step 1: Build a candidate list from competitors

Don't start from a brainstorm. ASO tools can list the keywords a competitor is indexed for. Steve says keywords he got from ChatGPT turned out to have no search volume in the store. If you need a tool, AppTweak was his pick in 2026 if you buy only one, and FoxData's free plan shows which keywords an app ranks for.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bV5_OwDB35o

*Video: The Most Important Element of App Store Optimization (ASO Keyword Research), App Masters.*

Pull keywords from two kinds of apps.

**Large competitors** give you the broadest list. Export everything.

**Small apps that rank well** tell you more. For a "calorie tracker" search, Steve looks past [Cal AI](/en/app-revenue/cal-ai) (about 200,000 ratings in his example) and MyFitnessPal (about 2.1 million) to Calorie AI, with about 4,000. Those big counts have grown since: the search results in Step 3 show 374K and 2.4M. An app with few ratings that still ranks may be showing you a keyword you can reach too.

Then cut hard. One public audit went from about 600 candidates to 200, then to 11 focus keywords, crossing out terms on relevance and search score. Keep highly relevant terms even when the score is low.

For a subscription app, add one more filter here. Ask whether someone searching this phrase has a problem they would pay for every month. Steve argues that "deep breathing" or "anxiety relief" shows more intent than "meditation", even with fewer searches. A subscription needs a payer, and a keyword only delivers a visitor.

## Step 2: Filter with tool scores, and don't trust them too far

Most ASO tools show two numbers: a search score and a difficulty score. App Masters uses both, and its advice has moved around.

| Video date | Search score App Masters suggests | Difficulty |
|---|---|---|
| Feb 2025 | 30 or more, 25 can work, avoid the low 20s | Low ASOMobile complexity |
| Apr 2025 | 25 to 39 | Complexity under 4 |
| Nov 2025 | Filter at 20 or more, start at 20 to 30, move up | Low |
| Feb 2026 | 30 or more, then 5 to 20 if that fails | As low as possible |
| Aug 2026 | About 30, 25 to 28 can work, 20 or less is poor | Complexity under 3 |
| Sep 2026 | 30 to 40 | AppRadar difficulty under 40 |

Read this table as a range. Scales differ between tools, so complexity under 3 and difficulty under 40 can't be compared directly. Steve also says he can't explain what the search score means in real searches, and that Apple doesn't define it. He treats daily search estimates as a barometer and calls tool difficulty a guess.

Tools also disagree. In App Masters' own 2026 comparison, one keyword got similar scores in three tools and a far lower one in a fourth. That covered one keyword on one app, so it says little about which tool is right. App Masters' working habit is more useful: check two tools and trust a score more when they agree.

Use scores only to drop obvious misses. A sensible start is a search score of 20 or more and the lower half of your tool's difficulty range. Treat that as a starting point and adjust it as you learn. Keep a lower-scoring term if relevance is very high, and cut terms that every tool rates as hard. Everything else goes to Step 3, where you look at the real results.

What if nothing clears the bar? Steve's advice in 2025 was that if you can't find keywords above 20, look at other channels. In 2026 he also described a fallback: many very low-score keywords. He reports one client ranking first on 92 keywords with a score of 5 and earning $2,000 to $3,000 a month. Be careful with that figure. His own videos say tools have shown 5 for keywords that were really higher, so those keywords may not have been as small as the score suggests.

## Step 3: Check the real search results

We think this step matters most. It is the only one that uses what people actually see.

[US App Store search results for calorie tracker, showing app names, subtitles, rating counts and screenshots]

*US App Store results for "calorie tracker", November 2026. Each card shows the name, subtitle and rating count.*

Search each surviving keyword on an iPhone in your target store. Search cards cut off long names, so open each page to read the full name. Look at the top five to seven apps and note two things:

1. How many ratings do they have?
2. Is the keyword in their app name?

If the top apps have many ratings and use the keyword in their names, skip it. If the top apps have few ratings, or the exact phrase is missing from their names, you have a candidate. Steve describes a keyword that tools rated as competitive, but where no ranking app used it in the name. He reports that the app reached the top spot soon after launch.

Three traps to remove while you're there:

- **Brand terms.** Competitor keywords usually don't work, because people pick the brand they searched for. Apple's rules also bar competing app names from the keyword field.
- **Misspellings.** Type them on a real device. If the store corrects the word, the keyword is worthless.
- **Apple's own product names.** Skip terms like Voice Memos.

Also check whether brands own the term. In App Masters' examples, Otter ranks first for "AI notetaker" with a name that isn't tuned for it, and its brand name scores as high as the generic term. Steve says Calm and Headspace outscore "meditation" itself. His conclusion is that metadata is the main lever for apps without a known brand. Our read: if a known brand holds the top spots, your keyword work is unlikely to move it.

## Step 4: Choose a short list

Steve Young's rule of thumb is to find six to ten relevant keywords, then try to get two of them to number one. The number comes from what fits in the app name and subtitle of two localizations, which we cover below. The two are your real targets, and the rest are backups for later rounds. He says the rule comes from apps where he can see both rank and revenue, and he admits he doesn't know how other combinations perform.

We would record each one in a simple sheet:

| Keyword and role | Fit | Scores in two tools | Top 5 results |
|---|---|---|---|
| Your term: focus or backup | Relevance, and would a searcher pay? | Tool A, tool B | Rating range, how many use it in the name |

A written sheet matters more than its format. It records why you chose a term, so you can judge the decision later.

## Step 5: Place keywords in the app name, subtitle and keyword field

Put your first focus keyword in the app name and your second in the subtitle. The name should still hint at what the app does, and the subtitle should explain its value. Guideline 2.3.7 bars subtitles that reference other apps or make claims you can't verify.

[Cronometer App Store page showing its name, subtitle and ratings]

*Cronometer uses its name for the brand and a keyword, and its subtitle for more terms. US App Store, November 2026.*

Use the keyword field for the remaining relevant terms. Since Apple tells you not to repeat words from the name, subtitle or category, you lose nothing by removing them. That leaves more of the 100 characters for new words.

For long phrases, split them. App Masters' example puts parts of "chronic symptoms tracker" across the app name and subtitle, then moves the combination that shows movement into the app name in the next version.

The iOS description is not on Apple's list of text relevance fields, so write it for people. Apple notes that it is also used for web search results.

### The Spanish (Mexico) tactic

App Masters reports that the US store also reads the Spanish (Mexico) localization. So, it says, English keywords placed in that localization can help US rankings and give you a second app name, subtitle and keyword field.

Here is what we could check. Apple's localization table lists Spanish (Mexico) among nine additional languages for the United States. Apple's help pages also say, using French as the example, that people can search with localized keywords in every country or region where the App Store supports that language. So the mechanism fits Apple's documentation.

Apple does not say that English words in a Spanish localization will rank in the US, or how they would be weighted. That part is App Masters' report only. In 2025 Steve said adding English to all nine languages expands indexing. In 2026 he said the others do less than Spanish (Mexico). Neither claim comes with public data.

If you try it, keep two limits in mind. Apple shows a localization to people whose language settings match it, so Spanish-speaking users may see that English text. In Mexico, Spanish (Mexico) is the default language. If you have a real audience there, this trade-off may not be worth it. Keep the terms accurate as well, because guideline 2.3.7 still applies.

## Step 6: Work in rounds

We found no tested schedule for updates, so work in rounds: push two focus keywords, read the data, then swap in a backup if they stall. Test your highest-scoring keyword first, because you can't know in advance how the algorithm will treat your app.

For each round, record rank, product page views, downloads and trial starts before you change anything. Change one set of metadata at a time. Otherwise you can't tell which change did what.

Decide what success means before you start. In February 2025, Steve said the goal was number one. Later videos accept the top two or three, while keeping number one as the goal. His own project shows why this matters. In the first month of a public build, Thumsters moved from 48th to 7th for "chores tracker", and App Masters reports that downloads barely changed. He says he wouldn't expect a download jump from that move. It is one app and one month, without revenue figures, so it can't prove the rule. It does show that a better rank alone may not mean much.

Set your expectations for the channel too. Steve has said since 2025 that ASO is one slice of the pie, and that two keywords can stall at around $1,000 a month. He also launches new apps with ASO and Apple Ads together.

## What to avoid

Some tactics promise faster rank: paid keyword installs, fake or paid reviews, and using another brand's name to catch its searches. Avoid them. App Review Guideline 5.6.3 says manipulating charts, search, reviews or referrals isn't permitted. Apple warns that manipulated reviews and inflated rankings can lead to removal from the Apple Developer Program. Guideline 2.3.7 covers trademarked terms and popular app names in metadata. App Masters has moved away from some of its own older growth advice as Apple's enforcement changed, so a tactic that worked last year is not safe by default.

## Google Play

Evidence here is thin. App Masters says Play uses the title, short description and description, gives the description more weight, and cares more about retention. Don't assume iOS localization tactics carry over.

## Rank doesn't show revenue

Everything above moves rank and, with luck, downloads. Neither tells you who pays. A subscription app earns from trials that convert and renew, and two keywords with the same rank can send very different users.

Paid search gives you the clearest read on that. If you run Apple Ads on your candidate keywords, you can compare what each one brings after the install. Airbridge Core Plan attributes trial starts and subscriptions to campaigns across Google, Meta, Apple and TikTok, and the Revenue report shows which ones earn money. With Apple Ads Advanced and the Campaign Management API integration, you can see this by keyword. This covers paid keywords, not the terms people type before an unpaid install, so use it as a signal for which organic keywords deserve the effort. Core Plan starts with a 30-day free trial, then $40+/mo.

To see these ideas on real apps, browse our [ASO teardowns](/en/aso). Once a keyword brings people to your page, the listing has to convert them. Our [guide to screenshots, icon tests and ratings](/en/blog/app-store-listing-conversion-screenshots-icons-ratings) covers that next step.

## App Store Listing Conversion: Screenshots, Icon Tests and Ratings

URL: https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/app-store-listing-conversion-screenshots-icons-ratings
Language: English
Published: 2026-11-05
Author: Hyunjong Choi

Keywords get your app into search results. Your listing decides whether anyone installs it. A better page gets more from the traffic you already have, including the installs you pay for.

This guide covers the first three screenshots, how to test an icon, and when to ask for ratings. This method comes from App Masters, the App Store Optimization (ASO) agency and YouTube channel founded by Steve P. Young, checked against Apple's documentation. App Masters sells ASO services, some of its videos are sponsored, and its results are its own reported wins. So we separate what Apple documents, what App Masters reports and what we think. Treat every reported result here as one team's anecdote. This guide covers iOS. Google Play evidence in these sources is thin.

## What is known about conversion and rank

Apple lists downloads, ratings and reviews among the user behaviors that affect search results, and it says ratings and reviews influence rank, without giving a size for either effect. A better listing may help rank through more downloads, but we found no App Masters case that shows it, so judge listing work by what it does on the page.

## The first three screenshots

**Apple's facts.** You can show up to 10 screenshots. Depending on orientation, the first one to three appear in search results when you have no app preview, and Apple tells you to make them show the essence of your app. Guideline 2.3.3 says screenshots should show the app in use, not just title art, a login page or a splash screen.

**App Masters' view.** These first images carry most of the weight, since fewer people swipe further. Slots four to ten still help, but they deserve less of your time.

[Cronometer's first App Store screenshots]

*[Cronometer](/en/app-revenue/cronometer)'s first screen echoes "nutrition" and "tracker" from its subtitle, then shows the product. US App Store, November 2026.*

A simple working order for portrait screenshots:

| Slot | Job |
|---|---|
| 1 | Match the search and say what the app does |
| 2 | Show your clearest difference |
| 3 | Show a second difference, or proof |
| 4 onward | One benefit or feature per screen, as Apple advises |

Check all three at the size people see them. Reduce them to search-result size on a phone and try to read the captions.

### Slot 1: match the search

Line up the first screenshot with your app name and main keyword, using large text. The person searched for something, and the first image should confirm they found it. This matters more the more you rely on organic search.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=x41YQ11Regg

*Video: How to Create App Store Screenshots That Get More Downloads, App Masters.*

Apple's text relevance list doesn't include screenshots, so choose your caption for the person reading it.

One test for the first slot: if someone saw only this image, could they say what the app is for? A logo, a splash screen or a vague slogan fails that test.

### Slots 2 and 3: your difference and your proof

One public example is a cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) app. The losing version used general wording about calming anxiety. The winning version put "CBT" in the first caption, used Editor's Choice as social proof, and highlighted a conversational video therapy feature, with CBT journaling on the third screen. App Masters reports a 30% lift in downloads from this A/B test. Steve calls it an older case, and the video states neither sample size nor duration.

Read that result with care. The winner changed the wording, the selling points and the order at the same time, so nobody can say which change did the work. The losing version also had social proof, so the video can't show that proof made the difference. The app was also already first for "CBT" search. App Masters presents this as a win without changing keywords. That is true for metadata, but the caption did gain a keyword.

The more useful part is how they found the selling points. One came from using the app first-hand. The other came from asking the team which feature users loved. You can do both this week. Read your reviews and support tickets too, and note the phrases people repeat.

For proof, use real signals such as Editor's Choice or an award badge. Steve says faces in the first three screens help, but his own tests of people against interface shots had only just started, so test this before you rely on it. Keep any proof specific. Guideline 2.3 expects metadata to reflect the app accurately, and an invented badge is a risk as well as a weak signal.

### Captions: outcomes, not features

Steve's demonstration is small and clear. He rewrites a caption about sharing and exporting into one about sending files faster. That is his judgment, and it's untested.

[Calorie Counter screenshots with the captions Fast, Easy Food Tracking and Log Food with Meal Scanner in App Store search results]

*Search-size captions. "Log Food with Meal Scanner" names a feature. Ask what the user gets from it. US App Store, November 2026.*

Try this on each caption. Read the feature name, then ask what the user gets from it.

| Feature caption | Outcome caption (our examples) |
|---|---|
| Sleep tracking | See why you woke up tired |
| Budget categories | Know what you can spend today |
| Workout library | Finish a workout in 20 minutes |

Keep it short, and only promise what the app does. For health or money apps, be careful with claims, because guidelines limit what you can say.

### What to test next

Good test topics include brand design, seasonal art, orientation, captions, video and screenshot order. Two examples are humbling. In an Angry Birds test App Masters cites as featured by Apple, the standard screenshots beat the seasonal ones, and Steve's own reorder test on his app Paraphrase AI won by only a small margin.

On video, Steve says previews tend to help games and are usually unnecessary for other apps, and that he has seen them hurt. Note that a preview changes what appears in search, since Apple says screenshots fill those results when no preview is available. Previews autoplay on mute, so the opening seconds have to work without sound.

Expect many tests to end small or flat. Public case studies show winners.

## How to run an icon test with Product Page Optimization

Product Page Optimization (PPO) is Apple's built-in A/B test for your product page. It can test icons, screenshots and app previews.

[App Store Connect screen for a product page test with a treatment and the original page]

*A product page test in App Store Connect. Image: Apple.*

**Apple's rules:**

- You can test up to three treatments against your original.
- You can run one test at a time, for up to 90 days.
- You choose a traffic proportion. In Apple's example, a 30% proportion across three treatments shows each treatment to 10% of traffic.
- Alternate icons must be in the binary (the app build) of the published app version. Tests without icons can go to review without a new version.
- New metadata in a treatment needs App Review approval before the test goes live.
- Apple recommends waiting for at least 90% confidence before acting on a result.
- Tests aren't available for custom product pages.
- Treatments reach people on iOS 15 and iPadOS 15 or later.

**The procedure.** This order follows an App Masters walkthrough with an indie developer, checked against Apple's help pages where they cover the step.

1. Choose one clear difference, something visible like color. Keep screenshots the same.
2. Add your current icon and each test icon to the Xcode asset catalog. Apple asks for 1024 by 1024 pixels.
3. In the walkthrough, the developer turns on "Include all app icon assets" in the app target's General settings. Apple's PPO pages don't name this setting, so check it against your Xcode version.
4. Archive the build and pass normal review. The icons have to be in the version on the App Store.
5. Create the test in App Store Connect. The App Icon tab appears only if the live build holds more than one icon. If you can't see it, go back to steps 2 and 3.
6. Pick your treatment count, traffic proportion and localizations, then send the treatment to review.
7. Avoid releasing a version that changes the tested assets, because Apple warns this may affect results.

The walkthrough also warns that an unfinished draft blocks new uploads, so plan your order of work before you start.

**Check your traffic first.** This is where many small apps should stop and think. Apple's setup screen estimates how long a test may take. Each extra treatment makes it longer, and Apple warns you may not reach your goal within 90 days. If the estimate is out of reach, use one treatment and a large visual difference, or spend your time on something else.

In the walkthrough, the test was on a pre-order app and the result had zero confidence. The people in the video still picked a direction from it. We don't treat that as evidence that any icon wins. Zero confidence is noise, whatever the percentage on screen says. Icon advice from Apple's design guidelines is safer ground: one clear idea, no needless detail, and legible at small sizes.

## When to ask for ratings

This is the part of the App Masters advice that has changed most, so check the date on any video you follow.

[The iOS rating prompt with five stars, Cancel and Submit]

*The system rating prompt. Image: Apple.*

| Video date | What App Masters advised |
|---|---|
| Jan to Jun 2025 | Ask early, in the first experience |
| Aug to Sep 2025 | Ask after the paywall or trial start, or before the paywall in onboarding |
| Oct to Nov 2025 | Says some apps were getting warnings from Apple, and drops rating prompts from its checklist |
| Feb 2026 | Stop asking after onboarding or the paywall. Ask after a win moment (a moment when the user has just got value), or on the second or third session |

Follow the latest version. Avoid first launch, onboarding and the moment right after the paywall.

The old advice rested mainly on one case. A four-year-old utility app moved its prompt to just after trial start. App Masters reports monthly ratings going from about 50 or 70 to about 400, with the average rising from 4.3 to 4.5. That is a before and after comparison with no control group, and Steve calls it an old case. Our read is that the prompt also changed who was answering, since it reached only people who had just started a trial. So the higher average may reflect a different sample, not a better app.

**Apple's rules:**

- The system prompt can appear up to three times in a 365-day period, and people can turn these prompts off.
- Use Apple's API. Guideline 5.6.1 disallows custom review prompts.
- Guideline 3.2.2 says you can't force a rating or review to unlock features or content.
- Apple warns against filtered or incentivized feedback. Asking only happy users is not a safe workaround.
- Apple's design guidance says to wait until people have shown engagement, and to avoid first launch, onboarding and interruptions. It suggests leaving a week or two between requests.
- Apple's StoreKit guide adds two details. Don't show the prompt right at launch, even on a later launch. Don't trigger it from a button tap. For a "Rate us" button, link to your App Store page instead.

Apple's guide does not contradict the second or third session idea, but it changes how you apply it. Don't fire the prompt when session two opens. Wait for a natural stop within that session.

**Pick a win moment for your app.** Finishing a game level or logging a first habit are two examples. For a subscription app, think of the first time the product delivers its promise: a completed workout, a finished lesson, a first useful report. Show the prompt on the screen after that moment, once the task is done.

With only three prompts a year, spend them well. Apple's example waits for four completions and calls that number arbitrary. If most users only get there once, ask after the first.

Keep your goal in proportion. Steve calls chasing rating counts vanity, and suggests aiming for 100 ratings, then 1,000. His rule of thumb is that about 1% of downloads leave a rating. He also believes ratings help paid campaigns, while saying this is his opinion.

## Downloads are not subscribers

A listing test tells you which page got more installs. It doesn't tell you which page brought people who pay. PPO measures page conversion, and the screenshot videos stop at the download.

A sharper promise can bring more installs and fewer subscribers. So the question to carry past every win is simple: did trial starts and paid conversions rise too?

This is easier to answer for traffic you pay for. Airbridge Core Plan attributes trial starts and subscriptions to campaigns across Google, Meta, Apple and TikTok. The Revenue report and Funnel report show which campaigns lead to paying users. With Apple Ads Advanced and the Campaign Management API integration, you can break that down by keyword. Compare trial and paid rates for the same campaign before and after the listing change. Core Plan starts with a 30-day free trial, then $40+/mo. Rank and download counts won't give you that view.

To see these ideas on real apps, browse our [ASO teardowns](/en/aso). If you're still working on how people find you, start with our [keyword research guide](/en/blog/app-store-keyword-research-subscription-apps).

## How Do I Know Which UGC Video Brought Paying Subscribers?

URL: https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/track-ugc-paying-subscribers
Language: English
Published: 2026-11-05
Author: Hyunjong Choi

Airbridge tracks the full path from a UGC video to a paying subscriber. You assign each creator or video a unique tracking link, and Airbridge attributes installs, trial starts, and subscriptions back to that specific piece of content. You see not just which video drove downloads, but which one drove revenue.

## Why install count is misleading for UGC

UGC campaigns generate installs cheaply, but installs alone tell you almost nothing about which creator content is worth paying for. A TikTok video from one creator might drive 5,000 installs with a 1% trial-to-paid rate. Another creator's video might drive 800 installs with a 15% trial-to-paid rate. If you optimize by install volume, you keep spending on the first creator and drop the second. That is the exact wrong decision.

The problem is that most teams track UGC performance with UTM parameters or platform-level metrics (views, clicks, installs). These break the moment a user closes the browser, reinstalls, or converts to a paid subscription days later. The gap between "someone tapped a link" and "someone started paying monthly" is where attribution tools earn their value.

To track UGC paying subscribers, you need a system that follows each user from video tap through app install, trial start, and first subscription payment, and ties all of those events back to the specific creator and specific video that started the journey.

## How to set up UGC tracking with Airbridge

Airbridge uses [branded short links](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/track-tiktok-creator-app-installs) to attribute installs and downstream events to individual creators or videos. Here is how to set it up:

**1. Create a unique tracking link for each creator or video.**
In the Airbridge dashboard, create a custom channel tracking link for every piece of UGC content. Airbridge also generates a short link, which you can brand with a custom domain. Use the link's parameters to identify the channel, the creator (Campaign), and the video (Ad Creative). When a creator posts multiple videos, each video gets its own link.

**2. Add a deep link so new users land on the right screen.**
When a user taps a tracking link, gets redirected to the App Store or Google Play, installs the app, and opens it for the first time, Airbridge matches that first open back to the original tap. This attribution does not depend on deep linking. Deferred deep linking is a separate step that sends new users to the right screen after install, and it works for 1 hour after the click.

**3. Track the standard subscription events.**
Airbridge has 25 standard events, and Core uses standard events only. The ones that cover the subscription funnel are Install, Sign Up, Start Trial, Subscribe, and Unsubscribe. Events inside the attribution window (30 days after install by default, adjustable) tie back to the original tracking link, so you can see which creator's content led to users who actually subscribe. The Revenue Report works differently: it credits each revenue event to the user's most recent Start Event without applying that window, so later renewals still count.

**4. Connect your subscription billing tool.**

## Migration Checklist: Switching Without Breaking Attribution

Switching MMPs does not have to mean losing continuity. Follow this sequence:

1. **Audit your current setup.** List every SDK event you are actually firing, every postback URL configured, and every integration active. Most small teams discover they use only part of what is configured.

2. **Check your contract terms.** Look for auto-renewal clauses and cancellation windows. Some enterprise contracts auto-renew unless you give notice well before the renewal date. [Understanding no-lock-in billing](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/mmp-no-lock-in-auto-renewal) explains what to watch for.

3. **Set up the new MMP in parallel.** With Airbridge Core, a basic SDK install takes about 5 minutes. Install the SDK alongside your existing MMP so both collect data during a transition window. This lets you validate numbers before cutting over.

4. **Map your events.** Airbridge Core includes 25 standard events and does not include custom events. Map your existing event names to these standards. If you rely on custom events, evaluate whether you need Growth or whether those events were enterprise bloat you can drop.

5. **Configure your channels.** Set up attribution for your active channels, typically Google Ads, Meta Ads, Apple Ads, and TikTok. Configure postbacks in each ad platform to point to your new MMP.

6. **Set up deep links.** Migrate your deep linking and branded link configurations. Test every major user flow: ad click to app open, web to app, deferred deep links for new installs.

7. **Validate during overlap.** Run both MMPs for at least two weeks. Compare install counts, event counts, and attribution breakdowns. Small discrepancies are normal due to methodology differences.

8. **Cut over.** Remove the old SDK, cancel the old contract, and confirm your new MMP is the single source of truth.

9. **Set up integrations.** Connect your analytics and BI tools. Airbridge Core includes 2 integrations; if you need more, Growth offers unlimited.

## How Attribution Integrations Work with RevenueCat

RevenueCat acts as the single source of truth for subscription status. When a user starts a trial, converts to paid, renews, or cancels, RevenueCat sends the event server to server to your connected MMP. The MMP then attributes that event back to the original install source, whether that was an Apple Ads campaign, a Meta ad, an organic search result, or a referral link.

The typical data flow looks like this:

1. A user clicks an ad and installs your app.
2. The MMP SDK records the install and attributes it to the correct campaign.
3. RevenueCat tracks the subscription lifecycle (trial start, conversion, renewal, billing issue, cancellation, expiration).
4. RevenueCat sends each event to your MMP via the integration.
5. The MMP ties revenue and retention data back to the original campaign, giving you cost-per-trial, cost-per-conversion, and LTV by channel.

This loop lets subscription app teams shift budget toward the campaigns that drive long-term subscribers rather than just installs.

- **Cross-platform analysis.** Have an agent compare performance across Google Ads, Meta Ads, Apple Ads, and TikTok without switching between tabs.
- **Event and funnel checks.** Query event counts or conversion rates without writing SQL or navigating complex UIs.

MCP turns your attribution platform into something an AI agent can operate, which reduces the manual overhead that slows down growth teams.

When a user sees a Spark Ad, taps through, and installs your app, Airbridge attributes that install to the TikTok campaign and ad group and shows the full funnel from install through trial start to paid subscription.

To measure TikTok Spark Ads for a mobile app, you set up three things: install the Airbridge SDK in your app, link TikTok as a channel in the Airbridge dashboard, and turn on cost integration. You handle Spark Ad authorization codes in TikTok Ads Manager, not in Airbridge. After that, Spark Ad data flows into the same attribution reports you use for your other channels.

## What are TikTok Spark Ads

Spark Ads are TikTok's native ad format that lets brands boost existing organic TikTok posts, either their own or a creator's, as paid advertisements. Unlike standard in-feed ads that are built from scratch in the TikTok Ads Manager, Spark Ads use real posts that already live on TikTok. The post retains its original likes, comments, and shares, and any new engagement from the ad goes back to the original post.

This makes Spark Ads popular for mobile app campaigns because they feel less like ads and more like organic content. Views, likes, comments, shares, and follows earned while the post is boosted are credited to the original post.

For measurement purposes, the key difference is that Spark Ads carry the creator's identity. The ad needs to be authorized by the creator through an authorization code, and measurement runs through the advertiser's MMP (mobile measurement partner) like Airbridge.

## How Spark Ad measurement works through an MMP

TikTok Spark Ads are measured the same way as any other TikTok ad campaign, through an MMP integration. The MMP receives attribution data from TikTok and matches it to in-app events.

Here is the flow:

1. **Ad click.** A user sees your Spark Ad on TikTok and taps through to the App Store or Google Play.
2. **The MMP collects the touchpoint.** Airbridge collects TikTok touchpoints through the SAN API and through Airbridge tracking links, which TikTok applies automatically.
3. **User installs and opens the app.** The MMP SDK detects the first open and matches it to the TikTok click using deterministic or probabilistic matching.
4. **Post-install events are attributed.** The MMP tracks subsequent events (registration, trial start, paid subscription) inside the attribution window and attributes them to the TikTok campaign and ad group.
5. **Cost data syncs automatically.** The MMP pulls cost data from TikTok so you can calculate CPI, cost per trial, and ROAS without manual spreadsheet work. In Airbridge, cost data updates every 4 hours.

Spark Ads run through the same TikTok integration as standard in-feed ads. To compare the two in your reports, run them in separate ad groups with clear names and group by ad group.

## Step-by-step setup: measuring Spark Ads with Airbridge

### 1. Install the Airbridge SDK

Add the Airbridge SDK to your iOS and Android app. The SDK tracks installs, sessions, and the standard in-app events you send. A basic install takes about 5 minutes.

### 2. Define your in-app events

Set up the events you want to attribute back to TikTok. Airbridge has 25 standard events, and Core uses standard events only. They include:

- Install and Open
- Sign Up
- Start Trial
- Subscribe
- Unsubscribe
- Order Complete for in-app purchases

Each event flows through attribution automatically once your app sends it. If you use RevenueCat, Adapty, or Superwall, first purchases, trial conversions, and renewals all arrive as Subscribe, so you read trial-to-paid in the Funnel Report as the share of Start Trial users who reach Subscribe.

### 3. Connect TikTok as a channel in Airbridge

In TikTok Ads Manager, go to Tools > Events, connect your app, and select Airbridge as the mobile measurement partner. Then, in the Airbridge dashboard, go to Integrations > Ad Channel Integration > TikTok For Business, enable channel integration, and register your TikTok App ID. This connection enables:

- Click attribution
- In-app event postbacks to TikTok
- Campaign and ad group reporting

### 4. Turn on cost integration

Cost integration is separate from channel integration. On the TikTok For Business page in Airbridge, open the Cost Integration tab, switch on the toggle, and add your ad account. You do not need to add a tracking link by hand: since April 2025, TikTok applies Airbridge tracking links automatically.

### 5. Set up the Spark Ad in TikTok Ads Manager

In TikTok Ads Manager, create your campaign and use the creator's authorized post as the ad creative. You will need the authorization code from the creator whose post you are boosting. Put each boosted post in its own ad group with a clear name so you can find it in Airbridge reports.

### 6. Verify data is flowing

After the campaign goes live, check the Airbridge Actuals Report. You should see TikTok installs appear once the campaign gets traffic. Cost data can take up to 4 hours. Verify that post-install events (trial starts, subscriptions) are also being attributed.

## What metrics you can see

Once Spark Ads are measured through Airbridge, you get the same reporting depth as any other channel:

**Acquisition metrics.** Installs, CPI (cost per install), and click-through rates by TikTok campaign and ad group. Cost data does not reach the creative level. With one boosted post in each ad group and clear names, you can see which creator content drives the most installs.

**Funnel metrics.** The full conversion path from Install to Start Trial to Subscribe. Airbridge Funnel Reports show where users drop off and which Spark Ad groups bring users who actually convert to paying subscribers.

**Revenue metrics.** ROAS (return on ad spend) calculated automatically using cost data synced from TikTok and revenue events from your app. Airbridge Predictive LTV estimates user value up to day 180 by multiplying a predicted user lifetime by ARPDAU, so you can estimate Spark Ad campaign profitability before actual renewal data matures. It needs at least 30 users in the cohort and a date range that starts at least 3 days ago (13 days is recommended).

**Retention metrics.** Day-1, Day-7, and Day-30 retention rates by TikTok campaign and ad group. Airbridge Retention Reports let you compare how well Spark Ad users retain compared to users from other channels.

**Cross-channel comparison.** Since Airbridge tracks all your channels in one dashboard, you can directly compare Spark Ad performance against your Google, Meta, and Apple Ads campaigns using the same attribution methodology.

## Does RevenueCat Do Attribution or Do I Need a Separate Tool?

Author: Hyunjong Choi

RevenueCat manages subscriptions and in-app purchases but does not do ad attribution. You need a separate mobile measurement partner (MMP) like Airbridge to connect ad clicks to installs and subscriptions. Airbridge integrates with RevenueCat on the Core Plan ($40+/mo). RevenueCat sends subscription events to Airbridge, which ties them to the ad campaign that drove the install.

## What RevenueCat Does vs What an MMP Does

RevenueCat and an MMP handle two distinct parts of the subscription business. RevenueCat sits between your app and the app stores, managing the purchase layer. An MMP sits between your ad campaigns and your app, tracking where users came from and what they did after install.

| Responsibility | RevenueCat | MMP (e.g., Airbridge) |
|---------------|-----------|----------------------|
| Purchase validation and receipt handling | Yes | No |
| Entitlement management | Yes | No |
| Cross-platform subscription status | Yes | No |
| Paywall configuration and A/B testing | Yes | No |
| Subscription revenue analytics | Yes | Yes (per campaign/channel) |
| Ad click to install attribution | No | Yes |
| Campaign-level revenue reporting | Only from attribution data it receives | Yes |
| Deep linking from ads | No | Yes |
| Fraud detection on installs | No | Yes (Airbridge: Growth Plan) |
| Apple Ads and ad network postback handling | No | Yes |
| Predictive LTV | Prediction Explorer chart | Yes (Airbridge: up to day 180, by acquisition source, dashboard only) |

RevenueCat tells you how much revenue you earn. An MMP tells you which campaigns produced that revenue. RevenueCat attribution is limited to the data it receives: what Apple returns for Apple Search Ads and any final campaign values you send it. Without both, you cannot calculate true return on ad spend for subscription products.

## How RevenueCat and an MMP Work Together

The integration between RevenueCat and an MMP follows a straightforward data flow:

1. A user clicks an ad, and the MMP SDK records the attribution source at install.
2. The user opens the app, browses your paywall, and starts a trial or subscribes.
3. RevenueCat processes the purchase and sends the subscription event (trial start, conversion, renewal, cancellation) to the MMP via server-to-server integration.
4. The MMP matches the subscription event to the original ad click, giving you campaign-level subscription metrics.

This means you can answer questions like "which Google Ads campaign drives the most trial-to-paid conversions" or "what is the 90-day LTV of users acquired from Apple Ads." RevenueCat does not determine which ad drove an install, so it cannot answer these questions on its own across your paid channels.
