## I Want to See Install, Trial Start, and First Subscription for Each Creator in One Funnel

URL: https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/creator-install-trial-subscription-funnel
Language: English
Published: 2026-11-05
Author: Hyunjong Choi

Airbridge's Funnel Report shows install → trial start → first subscription for each creator in a single view. You assign each creator a tracking link, and the funnel breaks down by that link, so you see exactly how many of Creator A's installs started a trial and how many went on to subscribe. The Revenue Report, grouped the same way, adds the revenue.

The Funnel Report is included in Airbridge's Core Plan ($40+/mo after a 30-day free trial). Core has 25 standard events, including Install, Start Trial, and Subscribe, so you can build a creator install trial subscription funnel without custom events, which are Growth only.

## How to set it up

### Step 1: Create a tracking link for each creator

In the Airbridge dashboard, go to Tracking Link > Link Generation > Custom Channels and create a link for every creator you work with. Enter a channel name such as `creators` and put the creator's name in the Campaign field. Airbridge also creates a short link and a QR code. The campaign value ties downstream events back to that specific creator.

If you are running ten creators this month, you create ten links. When a user taps Creator A's link, Airbridge attributes the install (and the events after it, inside the attribution window) to Creator A's campaign. The window is 30 days after install by default, and you can change it. The Revenue Report works differently: it credits each revenue event to the user's most recent Start Event without applying that window, so later renewals still count. This is what makes the per-creator breakdown possible: one link per creator, one attribution chain per user.

For a walkthrough of setting up creator-specific tracking links for subscription apps, see [Track Creator Campaigns for Subscription Apps](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/track-creator-campaigns-subscription-app).

### Step 2: Instrument the three funnel events

Airbridge's SDK includes standard events for install, trial start, and subscription. Install is captured automatically when the SDK initializes. For trial start and first subscription, you send the corresponding standard events from your app code when those actions happen.

A typical implementation looks like this:

- **Install.** Automatic via SDK. No code needed.
- **Trial start.** Send the Start Trial standard event (`airbridge.startTrial`) when the user begins a free trial.
- **First subscription.** Send the Subscribe standard event (`airbridge.subscribe`) when the first paid charge goes through.

Because these are standard events in Airbridge's taxonomy, the Funnel Report recognizes them without additional mapping.

If you use RevenueCat, Adapty, or Superwall, skip the SDK code for these two events. The integration sends them, and sending them both ways double counts. With these integrations, initial purchases, trial conversions, and renewals all arrive as Subscribe, so there is no separate trial-to-paid event. You read trial-to-paid from the funnel: it is the share of Start Trial users who reach the Subscribe step.

### Step 3: Build the funnel in the Funnel Report

Open the Funnel Report in the Airbridge dashboard. Add three steps:

1. Install
2. Start Trial
3. Subscribe

Then group by Campaign. The report renders a per-creator funnel showing how many installs each creator drove, how many of those installs started a trial, and how many of those trials reached Subscribe. Each user counts once per step, so renewals do not inflate it.

You can also set a conversion window of 1 to 180 days. It runs from the first step, so make it longer than your trial. Users who buy without a trial skip the Start Trial step, so run a second funnel of Install → Subscribe to count them.

For a step-by-step guide on building this exact funnel, see [Funnel: Install to Subscription](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/funnel-install-to-subscription).

## What this tells you that install counts alone do not

When you only track installs per creator, you are measuring reach, not value. A creator with 5,000 installs and a 2% subscription rate generates fewer paying users than a creator with 1,000 installs and a 15% subscription rate.

The funnel view answers questions that install counts cannot:

- **Which creators drive users who actually pay?** Install volume does not predict subscription revenue. The funnel shows which creators attract users who move through the entire journey.
- **Where does each creator's audience drop off?** If Creator A has a strong install-to-trial rate but a weak trial-to-subscription rate, the issue might be in onboarding or paywall design for that audience, not the creator's content.
- **Is a creator worth renewing?** Comparing cost per paid subscriber across creators is only possible when you can see subscriptions attributed to each one. Upload each creator's fee with CSV Cost Data Upload, with the creator in the campaign column, and Actuals shows CPI and other cost metrics per creator. Install-based CPI alone hides this.
- **How does creator performance compare to paid ads?** When your ad channels (Google Ads, Meta Ads, Apple Ads, TikTok) and creators all feed into the same Funnel Report, you can compare them side by side on the same metrics.

Planfit used this kind of event-level optimization, testing creatives and tracking through to free trial starts, and reduced their customer acquisition cost by 40% ([Planfit case study](https://www.airbridge.io/en/case-studies/planfit-app-event-optimization-free-trial)). ## Comparison with doing this manually

You can approximate a per-creator funnel without Airbridge, but it takes significantly more work and produces less reliable results.

### The manual approach

1. **UTM parameters + analytics tool.** Tag each creator's link with UTM parameters. Use your analytics tool (Google Analytics, Mixpanel, Amplitude) to track installs by UTM source.
2. **Match installs to trial starts.** Export install data and trial-start data, then join them on user ID. This requires your analytics tool to capture both events and maintain a consistent user identity across them.
3. **Match trial starts to subscriptions.** Pull subscription data from your payment provider (App Store Connect, Google Play Console, or RevenueCat) and join it to your trial-start data. This is the hardest join because payment platforms use their own transaction IDs, not your analytics user IDs.
4. **Aggregate by creator.** Once you have matched all three events per user, group by the original UTM source to get per-creator numbers.

### Where the manual approach breaks down

| | Manual (UTM + joins) | Airbridge Funnel Report |
|---|---|---|
| Attribution accuracy | Relies on UTM persistence; breaks on app reinstall, device switch, or delayed install | Device ID matching and probabilistic modeling |
| User identity | Must maintain consistent IDs across analytics, app, and payment platforms | Airbridge ID consolidates device and user IDs |
| Time to build | Hours to days per report; requires data engineering work | Minutes; select events and grouping in the dashboard |
| Ongoing maintenance | Breaks when schemas change; manual re-export each period | Automatic; saved reports update with new data |
| Conversion windows | Must be calculated manually in SQL or spreadsheets | Configurable in the report UI |
| Cross-channel comparison | Requires exporting and normalizing data from each ad platform separately | All channels in one report, same metrics |

The manual approach can work for a one-time analysis, but it is not sustainable for ongoing creator program management. Every time you add a new creator or change your event schema, the joins need to be rebuilt.

For more on tracking creator-driven subscribers in a single tool, see [Track UGC to Paying Subscribers](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/track-ugc-paying-subscribers).

It stores attribution data it receives, such as what Apple returns for Apple Search Ads, but you need an MMP to close that loop across your paid channels. RevenueCat sends the subscription data; the MMP connects it to the acquisition source.

### Can I use Predictive LTV with RevenueCat data?

Airbridge offers Predictive LTV up to day 180 on the Core Plan. It multiplies a machine-learning prediction of user lifetime by average revenue per daily active user (ARPDAU) and shows the result in the dashboard by acquisition channel. It is not sent to ad networks. This helps you make budget decisions based on projected value rather than short-window ROAS metrics.

### How long does it take to set up an MMP with RevenueCat?

The RevenueCat side of any integration is configured in minutes through the RevenueCat dashboard. A basic Airbridge SDK install takes about 5 minutes. Other MMPs vary. Plan testing time to verify that events flow correctly before using the data for campaign decisions.

Historical data stays in the old MMP. RevenueCat's integrations are configured on RevenueCat's side, so switching means enabling the new MMP integration and providing connection credentials. New subscription events then route to the new platform. Past data does not migrate automatically, so export what you need before your old contract ends.

The best cost per install does not always come from the best channel. ## Why CPI Alone Is Misleading

| Metric | What It Tells You | What It Misses |
|---|---|---|
| Cost per install (CPI) | How much you pay to acquire one download | Whether that user ever opens the app or pays |
| Cost per trial start | How much you pay per user who begins a trial | Whether trials convert to paid |
| Cost per paying subscriber | How much you pay per revenue-generating user | This is the metric that matters |
| ROAS (return on ad spend) | Revenue earned per dollar spent on ads | Long-tail revenue beyond the measurement window |

A low CPI can mask poor channel quality. If 90% of installs from a cheap channel churn within a day, the true acquisition cost per retained user is far higher than the headline number. Evaluating channels means following users past the install.

## How to Get Campaign-Level Revenue When You Use Adapty

URL: https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/adapty-campaign-level-revenue
Language: English
Published: 2026-11-05
Author: Hyunjong Choi

Airbridge integrates with Adapty to connect subscription revenue to the ad campaigns that drove each user. Once the integration is active, Adapty sends subscription events to Airbridge, which attributes each trial start, conversion, and renewal to a specific Google Ads, Meta Ads, Apple Ads, or TikTok campaign.

This lets you see which campaigns actually generate paying subscribers rather than just installs, so you can shift budget toward the campaigns that produce real revenue.

## How the Adapty + Airbridge Integration Works

Adapty manages your paywalls, subscription offers, and billing events. When a user starts a trial, converts to paid, renews, or cancels, Adapty records that event. The integration forwards these events to Airbridge server to server.

Airbridge already knows which campaign brought each user to your app. It tracked the install attribution when the user first opened the app. When Adapty's subscription events arrive, Airbridge matches them to the original install source using the device ID and user ID, which is why your app passes the Airbridge device ID to Adapty.

The result is a full picture. For example, you might see that Campaign X on Google Ads brought 500 installs, 120 started a trial, 45 converted to paid, and they generated $2,700 in revenue over the first 90 days.

## What Data Flows Between Adapty and Airbridge

Adapty sends subscription lifecycle events to Airbridge, including:

- **Trial started** (Start Trial): a user began a free trial
- **Initial purchase** (Subscribe): a user bought a subscription
- **Trial converted** (Subscribe): a trial user became a paying subscriber
- **Subscription renewed** (Subscribe): an existing subscriber renewed for another billing period
- **Auto-renew turned off** (Unsubscribe): a user turned off auto-renew

These map to Airbridge standard events, so they work on the Core Plan. All other Adapty events, such as billing issues and expirations, arrive as custom events, which require the Growth plan.

Airbridge takes each event and attributes it back to the campaign, ad group, and creative that originally drove the install. This means you can build reports in Airbridge that show revenue per campaign, per channel, or per country, all tied to real Adapty billing data.

## Step-by-Step: Connecting Adapty to Airbridge

1. **Create an Airbridge account.** Sign up at airbridge.io. The Core Plan has a 30-day free trial, then starts at $40+/mo with 500K data points per month, so you can test the integration before committing. No annual contract is required.

2. **Install the Airbridge SDK in your app.** Add the Airbridge SDK alongside your existing Adapty SDK. The Airbridge SDK handles install attribution and tracks which campaign brought each user. Pass the Airbridge device ID to Adapty with `setIntegrationIdentifier`, using the key `airbridge_device_id`, and log the same user ID in both tools.

3. **Copy your Airbridge credentials.** In the Airbridge dashboard, go to `Integrations` > `Third-party Integrations` and select `Adapty`. Copy the Airbridge app name and API token.

4. **Configure events in Adapty.** In the Adapty dashboard, go to `Integrations` > `Airbridge`, switch on the toggle, and paste the app name and token. Then turn on the event groups you want to forward (Subscriptions, Trials, and Issues) and click `Save`. On Core, you can leave Issues off. Trial and subscription events map to Airbridge standard events by default, so you do not need to map them yourself.

5. **Paste the Adapty API token into Airbridge.** Copy the Adapty API token from the same Adapty page. Paste it into the Adapty page in the Airbridge dashboard and click `Done`. This lets Airbridge send install attribution data back to Adapty.

6. **Verify the data flow.** Trigger a test subscription event in your app. Check the Airbridge dashboard to confirm the event arrived and was attributed to the correct campaign source.

7. **Build revenue reports.** Use Airbridge's Revenue Report with the Subscription Revenue (App) metric to see campaign-level revenue. Use the Funnel Report to visualize the path from install to trial to paid subscription.

## Why Campaign-Level Revenue Matters for Subscription Apps

Install counts alone tell you which campaign brought a download but not whether that user ever paid. For subscription apps using Adapty, this gap is significant because the value of a user unfolds over weeks and months.

With Airbridge attributing Adapty revenue back to campaigns, you can answer questions like:

- Which Google Ads campaigns produce the most subscription revenue over time?
- Are Meta Ads trials converting at a higher rate than Apple Ads trials?
- Which country and campaign combination has the highest revenue per install?

## MMP Pricing for Freemium Apps: How to Choose the Right Model

URL: https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/mmp-pricing-freemium-apps
Language: English
Published: 2026-11-05
Author: Luke

## MMP pricing for freemium apps: a buyer's guide

Freemium apps have a particular shape: lots of installs, lots of free users, and a small share who pay. That shape matters when you choose a mobile measurement partner (MMP), because many pricing models charge by volume. One freemium founder summed up his frustration: the cost per conversion was "getting out of hand," and "with a freemium model, the unit economics just don't make sense anymore."

The fix isn't always a cheaper tool. It's a pricing model that fits how your app makes money.

## The common pricing models

| Pricing model | You pay for | Fits best when | Watch out for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Per attributed install or conversion | Each install (or other conversion) credited to a paid source | You buy a modest number of high-value installs | High install volume with low pay rates; what counts as a "conversion" |
| Per monthly active user (MAU) | Each user active in a month | Small, engaged user base | Large free audiences that open the app often |
| Per data point or event | Each tracked event or data point | You can control how many events you track | Tracking many low-value events |
| Flat tier | A fixed monthly or annual fee up to a limit | Predictable volume | What happens when you pass the limit |

Most vendors combine these with a base fee, feature tiers and minimum terms.

  

[MMP pricing models for freemium apps: per attributed install or conversion, per monthly active user, per data point or event, and flat tier, with what you pay for, when each fits and what to watch out for]

## Why freemium apps feel pricing differently

A freemium app's revenue grows with **payers**. Many pricing models grow with **volume**: installs, active users or events. If 2% of installers ever pay, a model that bills every install means 98% of your billable units never bring revenue.

That's not a reason to avoid any model. It's a reason to estimate your costs with your own numbers before deciding.

## A simple worksheet

Fill in your own numbers for the next 12 months:

1.  **Installs per month**, split into paid and organic.
    
2.  **Monthly active users.**
    
3.  **Events per user per month** you actually need: install, onboarding complete, trial start, purchase, renewal. Skip low-value events.
    
4.  **Expected growth.** Plan for your best month, not your average.
    

Then ask each vendor to price the same scenario, and compare total cost per month and **cost as a share of revenue**.

## Questions to ask before you sign

-   **What exactly is billable?** Paid installs only, or organic too? Re-installs? Re-engagements? Web events?
    
-   **What does "conversion" mean in the contract?** Ask whether a billable conversion is an install, a re-engagement or an in-app event, and make sure the contract uses the same definition you discussed.
    
-   **What happens when you exceed your plan?** Is overage priced per unit, or does it move you to a new tier?
    
-   **Contract length.** Monthly or annual? Can you start small and upgrade?
    
-   **Included integrations.** Are the ad networks and your subscription platform included, or extra? Not sure you need an MMP next to your subscription platform? Read [Do You Need an MMP If You Use RevenueCat?](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/do-i-need-an-mmp-with-revenuecat)
    
-   **Free tier limits.** If there's a free plan, what are the limits, and what happens when you reach them?
    

## Match the model to your stage

-   **Pre-scale (under a few thousand paid installs a month):** look for low base fees, monthly terms and no long contract.
    
-   **Scaling freemium (high installs, low pay rate):** prefer models where cost tracks the events you choose, or where organic installs aren't billed.
    
-   **Mature (steady payer base):** negotiate on predictability: annual tiers with clear overage rules.
    

## Buyer's summary

-   MMPs usually price by attributed installs or conversions, monthly active users, data points or events, or fixed tiers.
    
-   For a freemium app, the key question is **what counts as billable, and does it grow faster than your revenue?**
    
-   Model your next 12 months of installs, events and active users, and compare the cost under each model before you sign.
    

## MMP pricing FAQ

### How do MMPs price their services?

Common models charge per attributed install or conversion, per monthly active user, per data point or event, or a flat tier, often with a base fee and minimum term.

### Which MMP pricing model is best for a freemium app?

Usually one where cost grows with the events that matter to revenue, not with every install or free user. Model your own numbers under each option before deciding.

### Are organic installs billable?

It depends on the vendor and plan. Ask directly, and get the answer in writing, since organic volume can be large for freemium apps.

### How much should an MMP cost as a share of revenue?

There's no fixed rule. Compare the tool's monthly cost with the decisions it improves, such as moving budget from channels with high cost per subscriber to channels with low cost per subscriber.

### Can I switch MMPs later?

Yes, but it takes planning: SDK changes, new links, ad network connections and a period of running both. Choosing a model that scales with you saves a migration later.

## Choosing with confidence

For freemium apps, the right MMP is the one whose bill grows with your revenue, not just your installs. Know what's billable, model your next 12 months, and ask the hard contract questions up front.

## Web-to-App Attribution: Connect Web Checkout and In-App Subscriptions

URL: https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/web-to-app-attribution-web-checkout
Language: English
Published: 2026-11-05
Author: Luke

## What web-to-app attribution means

More subscription apps now sell on the web as well as in the app. Some send ad traffic to a web paywall, some offer web checkout to existing users, and in the US, Apple's rules on linking from an app to web purchases changed in 2025 and are still evolving, so always check the current [App Review Guidelines](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/).

The catch is data. One founder described his setup: "Web payments go through Stripe and the mobile ones through the stores, so the conversion data lives in different places and I haven't joined it into one view."

**Quick answer**

-   Give every person **one user ID** that follows them from the web to the app.
    
-   Capture the ad or link source on the web page and attach it to that ID at checkout.
    
-   Pass the same ID into the app when the person signs in.
    
-   Combine web and in-app payments by user and by channel, so you can see cost per subscriber across both.
    

## The three web-to-app journeys

| Journey | What happens | Where data splits |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Web paywall first | Ad → web landing page → web checkout → download app → sign in | The payment is on the web; app usage is in the app |
| App first, web checkout later | Ad → install → in-app prompt → web checkout | The install source is in the app; the payment is on the web |
| Web lead, app purchase | Ad → web quiz or waitlist → install → in-app purchase | The ad click is on the web; the purchase is in the app |

In every case, the person is the same. The goal is to make your data agree.

  

[Web-to-app funnel example: Noom's trial flow starts with a web quiz on noom.com asking about the user's weight loss goal, before the app is downloaded]

_A web-first journey in practice: Noom starts its trial flow with a short quiz on its website, before anyone downloads the app. Source: Noom_

## Step 1: Capture the source on the web

Tag every link that sends people to your web pages with campaign parameters, such as UTMs or your attribution tool's link. On the landing page, store the source with the visitor's session. When the visitor signs up or pays, save that source with their account.

## Step 2: Use one user ID everywhere

Create the account before or during checkout, so the payment belongs to a user ID, not just an email. When the person opens the app, have them sign in, or open the app with a deep link that carries a one-time sign-in token. Now your web payment and your in-app activity share one ID.

## Step 3: Bring web and in-app payments together

You need one place where both kinds of payment sit on the same user:

-   Add the user ID to your web checkout records, for example as metadata on the payment.
    
-   Make sure your subscription platform or backend stores in-app purchases under the same user ID.
    
-   Combine them in your subscription platform, if it supports web payments, or in your own reporting.
    

One founder we talked with already writes web and store payments into one row per user. The missing piece, as he put it: the row "doesn't track where people came from yet, but it should." Add the source to that row and you have web-to-app attribution in its simplest form.

## Step 4: Attribute app installs from web pages

When a web page sends people to the App Store or Google Play, use a tracking link on the download button rather than a plain store link. A web-to-app attribution link credits the install to the web page and campaign, and can open the right screen after install. If people click your ads but never reach checkout or sign-up, [track every step between your ad and your app](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/ad-clicks-no-signups-funnel-tracking) to see where they drop off.

## Step 5: Report cost per subscriber across both

Once web and app payments share a user ID and a source, report:

| Channel | Spend | Web subscribers | In-app subscribers | Total subscribers | Cost per subscriber |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Meta → web paywall | $1,000 | 32 | 6 | 38 | $26.32 |
| TikTok → app install | $800 | 4 | 21 | 25 | $32.00 |
| Creator links | $500 | 9 | 17 | 26 | $19.23 |

_Numbers are illustrative._

  

[Web-to-app attribution example: web checkout and in-app subscribers counted together by channel, giving a cost per subscriber of $26.32 for a web paywall campaign, $32.00 for an app install campaign and $19.23 for creator links (illustrative)]

Without the join, the Meta campaign would look strong on the web and weak in the app, and the creator links would look weaker than they are.

## A note on fees and rules

Web checkout and in-app purchases have different fees, refund flows and rules, and those rules differ by country and change over time. Compare channels on **net** revenue, and check the current App Store and Google Play policies for your markets before linking to web purchases from inside your app.

## Web-to-app attribution FAQ

### How do I track subscriptions bought on the web and in the app together?

Use one user ID across both. Capture the ad source on the web, save it with the account at checkout, have users sign in to the app with the same account, and combine web and in-app payments by user.

### What is web-to-app attribution?

It connects a person's journey from a web page, such as a landing page or web paywall, to their install and activity in the app, so you can credit the right campaign for installs and purchases on both sides.

### Can US iOS apps link to web checkout?

On the US storefront, Apple's guidelines have allowed links and buttons to external purchase options since May 2025, but the related rules are still being settled in court and may change. Rules differ in other countries, so check Apple's current guidelines for each market before adding links.

### Should I send ad traffic to a web paywall or to the App Store?

Test both. Web paywalls give you more control over the offer and payment, while store installs are simpler for users. Compare them on cost per subscriber, not cost per click or install.

### Why do my web and app subscriber numbers double-count?

Usually because the same person exists under two IDs, one from web checkout and one in the app. Link them with sign-in or a deep link token so each person counts once.

## Before you launch a web paywall

Selling on the web and in the app is a growth opportunity, but only if your data follows the person, not the payment page. One user ID, a captured source and a combined report turn two half-funnels into one picture of which channels bring paying users.

More app teams build their own growth dashboards than ever. One founder described a React tool that pulls together subscription, App Store, product analytics and ad platform data. Another told us his team now handles most monitoring with dashboards they built using an AI assistant: "we claude-dashboard our way through most of our monitoring now :)". Others keep a strict spreadsheet updated every week.

Building has never been easier. The question is whether keeping it right every week is worth your team's time.

## What a growth dashboard needs to answer

Most subscription teams want the same handful of answers:

-   How much did we spend, by channel and campaign?
    
-   How many installs, trials and subscribers did each one bring?
    
-   What's our cost per trial and cost per subscriber by channel?
    
-   How much revenue did each cohort bring over time, after refunds?
    

The first and last questions are easy to build. The middle two need attribution: connecting each user to the campaign that brought them. That's also where numbers from different sources start to differ; here's [why ad platform and subscription dashboards don't match](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/ad-platform-vs-subscription-data-mismatch).

## The four hidden costs of building

| Hidden cost | What it involves |
| --- | --- |
| Attribution | Matching installs and events to campaigns, creators and links across iOS, Android and web, including privacy-protected data |
| Cost import | Pulling spend from every ad network's API, in the right currency and time zone |
| Definitions | Agreeing what counts as a trial, a subscriber and revenue (gross, net, after refunds) and keeping every chart consistent |
| Maintenance | Fixing breakages when an API changes, a token expires or an event name changes |

The first version takes a weekend. The ongoing cost is a few hours every week, usually from your most technical person.

  

[Build vs. buy an app growth dashboard: the four hidden costs of building one yourself are attribution, cost import, definitions and maintenance]

## When building makes sense

-   One or two paid channels, each with clear in-platform reporting.
    
-   A stable set of events and plans.
    
-   Someone on the team who likes owning data and has time for it.
    
-   Questions that are mostly about revenue and product, not about which campaign brought whom.
    

## When buying (or combining) makes sense

-   Three or more channels, or any creator and influencer spend.
    
-   You need user-level attribution across iOS, Android and web.
    
-   You want ad platforms to receive attributed events for optimization.
    
-   The dashboard broke more than once last quarter.
    
-   Your most technical person is spending more time on reporting than on the product.
    

Many teams combine both: an attribution tool handles the hard joins, and they still build custom views on top using exported data.

## A middle path

1.  **Keep your subscription platform as the revenue source of truth.**
    
2.  **Use an attribution tool for the user-to-campaign join** and for importing ad costs.
    
3.  **Export raw data** into your warehouse or spreadsheet.
    
4.  **Build your own views** for the questions unique to your business.
    

This keeps the flexibility of building without owning the parts that break most often.

## Decision summary

-   Build when you have one or two channels, a stable setup and someone who enjoys owning data.
    
-   Buy, or combine both, when you run several channels, pay creators, need user-level attribution across platforms, or find the dashboard breaking every few weeks.
    
-   The hard part isn't the charts. It's **attribution, cost import, definitions and maintenance**.
    

## Build vs. buy FAQ

### Should I build my own app marketing dashboard?

It can work well with one or two channels, stable events and someone to maintain it. As channels, creators and platforms grow, attribution and maintenance usually make a tool worth it.

### What's the hardest part of building a growth dashboard?

Attribution: connecting each user to the campaign, creator or link that brought them across platforms. Charts and revenue totals are the easy part.

### Can I combine an attribution tool with my own dashboard?

Yes. Many teams use an attribution tool for joins and cost import, then export raw data to build their own views.

### How do I know my homemade dashboard is no longer worth it?

When it breaks often, when someone spends hours a week maintaining it, or when it can't answer which campaigns bring your best subscribers.

### What data sources should a subscription app dashboard include?

Ad spend by campaign, attributed installs and events, subscription revenue and renewals from your subscription platform, and refunds.

## Our take

Building a dashboard is easy. Keeping attribution, costs and definitions right every week is the real work. Build what's unique to your business, and let a tool own the parts that break.

## Tracking setup checklist for Flutter, FlutterFlow and Expo apps

Many founders reach their first paid campaign the same way: the app is built, subscriptions work, and now it's time to grow. Several told us the same thing when we asked how they'd track ads: they hadn't figured it out yet, but planned to "before launching the ads."

That's the right instinct. One growth-minded founder put the rule in one line: "set up your tracking before you spend a single dollar on ads." Data you don't collect on day one can't be recovered later.

**The checklist.** Before your first campaign:

-   Decide a short list of events.
    
-   Add an attribution SDK the way your framework supports native code.
    
-   Connect your subscription platform.
    
-   Set up iOS privacy measurement and update your privacy policy.
    
-   Test the full path from a test ad click to a trial start.
    

  

[Tracking setup checklist for a first paid campaign on Flutter, FlutterFlow or Expo: decide your events, add attribution for your framework, connect your subscription platform, set up iOS privacy measurement, test the full path, then launch small and read cost per trial]

## Step 1: Decide your events

Keep it short. Four or five events cover most subscription apps:

| Event | When it fires | Why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| install / first open | First launch | The base of every funnel |
| onboarding_complete | Last onboarding screen | Early quality signal |
| start_trial | Trial confirmed by the store | The event most small campaigns should optimize for |
| purchase | First paid transaction | Revenue |
| renewal | Each renewal | Long-term value |

Use the same names everywhere: in your app, subscription platform, attribution tool and ad platforms.

## Step 2: Add attribution the right way for your framework

Attribution SDKs and ad platform SDKs include native code. How you add them depends on your stack:

-   **Flutter:** add the vendor's official Flutter plugin from pub.dev, then follow its iOS and Android setup steps (Info.plist, AndroidManifest, initialization in main.dart).
    
-   **FlutterFlow:** add the plugin as a dependency through custom code, and call it from a custom action at app start. Check that your FlutterFlow plan supports custom code before you commit to a tool.
    
-   **React Native with Expo:** Expo Go can't load custom native modules. Use a [development build](https://docs.expo.dev/develop/development-builds/introduction/) and the vendor's config plugin, then build with EAS.
    
-   **Bare React Native:** install the npm package and run the native install steps for iOS and Android.
    

Whichever you choose, prefer an SDK with official support for your framework. Community wrappers can lag behind native SDK updates.

  

[Expo documentation, Introduction to development builds: a development build is your own version of Expo Go where you can use any native libraries, and it is recommended when you want to release your own app to app stores]

_Expo recommends a development build when you need native libraries and plan to release to the app stores. Source: Expo documentation_

## Step 3: Connect your subscription platform

If you use RevenueCat, Adapty or Superwall, turn on its integration with your attribution tool. Subscription events such as trial conversions and renewals then flow to the campaigns that drove each user, server to server, without extra app code.

## Step 4: Set up iOS privacy measurement

-   **ATT prompt:** decide whether and when to show the App Tracking Transparency prompt. Show it after you've explained the value, not on the first screen.
    
-   **Privacy-preserving attribution:** Apple's [AdAttributionKit](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/adattributionkit) and SKAdNetwork measure ad conversions without the ATT prompt. Map your key events, especially trial start, into conversion values.
    
-   **Apple Ads:** collect the Apple Ads attribution token at first launch so installs from Apple Ads are tagged by campaign and keyword.
    
-   **Privacy policy and store labels:** update your privacy policy and the App Store and Google Play data disclosures to reflect the SDKs you add.
    

## Step 5: Test the full path

Before spending, run one end-to-end test:

1.  Tap a test tracking link on a real device.
    
2.  Install the app from the store or a test build.
    
3.  Complete onboarding and start a sandbox trial.
    
4.  Confirm in your attribution tool that the install and trial are credited to the test link.
    
5.  Confirm the trial start appears once, with the right timestamp, in each ad platform's event tools.
    

Fix anything that fires twice or not at all now. It's much harder once real money is flowing. If clicks still don't turn into sign-ups after launch, [track every step between your ad and your app](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/ad-clicks-no-signups-funnel-tracking) to find the drop.

## Step 6: Launch small, read cost per trial

Start with one channel and one campaign optimized for trial starts. After a week, read cost per trial. After the trial period, read cost per subscriber. Then decide where the next dollar goes.

## Setup FAQ

### What should I set up before running ads for my app?

A short event list, an attribution SDK, your subscription platform's integration, iOS privacy measurement, an updated privacy policy, and one end-to-end test from link tap to trial start.

### Can I add an attribution SDK to a FlutterFlow app?

Usually yes, by adding the vendor's Flutter plugin through custom code and initializing it in a custom action. Check your plan's custom code support first.

### Do attribution SDKs work with Expo?

Yes, with a development build. Expo Go can't run custom native modules, so use a development build and the SDK's config plugin.

### Do I need the ATT prompt to measure iOS ads?

No. Apple's privacy-preserving attribution frameworks work without it. The ATT prompt gives more detailed data for users who allow tracking.

### Which event should my first campaign optimize for?

For most trial-based subscription apps, the trial start: it predicts payment and happens often enough for ad platforms to learn.

## Launch day

Your first paid campaign is a test, and a test is only useful if you can read the result. Pick your events, add attribution the way your framework supports it, connect your subscription platform, handle iOS privacy, and test the whole path before you spend.

## Tracking Reddit and Indie Hackers posts: a five-step playbook

For many solo founders, community posting is the first growth channel: a build-in-public update on Indie Hackers, a helpful answer on Reddit, a launch on Product Hunt, a blog post that ranks. It's free, but it isn't cheap. It takes hours every week.

So it's worth knowing which posts actually bring users. One founder who posts several times a week drew a sharp line: "getting attention, becoming part of a community, and actually acquiring users are three very different things."

**The playbook in brief**

-   Treat every post as a small campaign.
    
-   Give each post its **own link** and keep a **post log** with dates.
    
-   Add one **onboarding question** that lists your communities.
    
-   Judge posts on **trial starts and subscribers, not upvotes or views**, and spend your limited hours on the communities and post types that convert.
    

## Why upvotes don't tell you much

Upvotes, likes and comments measure how a post landed with the community. They're a good signal for writing, but a weak signal for acquisition. A post can top a subreddit and bring no one who installs, while a modest reply in a niche thread brings three paying users. As one founder found when he checked where his sign-ups came from: "6 of my 8 signups last week came from comments on other people's posts."

## Step 1: One link per post

Use a separate link for each post or comment where you include a link, so you can see which one brought visitors and installs:

-   **For a web page:** add campaign parameters, for example utm\_source=reddit&utm\_campaign=r-productivity-2026-11-04.
    
-   **For an app store page:** use an App Store Connect [campaign link](https://developer.apple.com/help/app-store-connect-analytics/acquisition/campaign-links/) on iOS and a UTM-tagged Google Play link on Android, or one tracking link that routes each person to the right store.
    

One founder who started doing this put it simply: "giving each Reddit post and YouTube Short its own link makes sense. That would help me decide where to spend my limited time."

Always follow each community's rules on self-promotion and links. Many subreddits limit links or ban them in posts. Where links aren't allowed, the next two steps still work.

## Step 2: Keep a post log

A simple sheet with one row per post: date and time, community, post type (launch, update, answer, tutorial), link used, and the post's views or upvotes at 48 hours. The log lets you match trial-start spikes to posts, even for posts with no link.

## Step 3: Ask where people found you

## Subscription App Payback Period: What to Do When CAC Beats the First Payment

URL: https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/subscription-app-payback-period
Language: English
Published: 2026-11-05
Author: Luke

## Subscription app payback period, in plain math

One founder running Meta campaigns for an iOS subscription app summed up a common worry: "I'm struggling to understand how to make the campaigns profitable when the cost of acquiring a paying subscriber is higher than the revenue from their first payment."

That situation is normal for monthly plans and often fine. What matters is when the campaign pays back, and whether you can afford to wait that long.

**The math at a glance**

- Work out four numbers: **cost per subscriber**, **net revenue per payment** after store fees, **retention by month**, and how long you can afford to wait.

- Annual plans usually pay back on the first payment.

- Monthly plans pay back over several months, so payback depends on churn.

- A campaign is healthy if it pays back within the time your cash allows.

## Step 1: Cost per subscriber, not cost per install

Start from what you pay for each subscriber, not each install:

Cost per subscriber = cost per trial ÷ trial-to-paid rate

If a trial costs $8 and 35% of trials convert, each subscriber costs about $22.86.

## Step 2: Net revenue per payment

Use what you actually receive, after store fees and taxes collected by the store. For many subscription apps the store fee is 15%: Google Play charges 15% on [subscriptions](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/112622), and Apple charges 15% to members of its [Small Business Program](https://developer.apple.com/app-store/small-business-program/). Check the rate that applies to your account and region.

At a 15% fee:

| Plan    | List price | Net per payment |
|---------|------------|-----------------|
| Monthly | $7.99     | $6.79          |
| Annual  | $39.99    | $33.99         |

## Step 3: Annual plans: payback on the first payment

With a $22.86 cost per subscriber and $33.99 net from the first annual payment, the campaign pays back immediately, with $11.13 left over per subscriber. The real question for annual plans is renewal rate at month 12, which decides long-term value.

## Step 4: Monthly plans: payback depends on retention

For a monthly plan, the first payment ($6.79 net) covers less than a third of the $22.86 cost. Payback depends on how many subscribers keep paying. Here is an illustrative retention curve:

| Month | Still paying | Net revenue per original subscriber | Cumulative |
|-------|--------------|-------------------------------------|------------|
| 1     | 100%         | $6.79                              | $6.79     |
| 2     | 70%          | $4.75                              | $11.54    |
| 3     | 58%          | $3.94                              | $15.48    |
| 4     | 50%          | $3.40                              | $18.88    |
| 5     | 45%          | $3.06                              | $21.93    |
| 6     | 42%          | $2.85                              | $24.78    |

*Numbers are illustrative.*

[Subscription app payback period on a monthly plan: cumulative net revenue per original subscriber grows from $6.79 in month 1 to $24.78 in month 6, passing the $22.86 cost per subscriber in month 6 (illustrative)]

The campaign pays back in month 6. Whether that's good depends on your cash: if you can wait six months, it's a profitable campaign; if you need money back in 30 days, it isn't yet.

## Step 5: Decide what to change

If payback is too slow, you have four levers:

- **Lower cost per trial:** optimize campaigns for trial starts, test creatives, cut channels with high cost per subscriber.

- **Raise trial-to-paid:** improve onboarding and the paywall moment, remind users before the trial ends.

- **Shift the plan mix:** promote annual plans, which collect more up front.

- **Improve early retention:** months 2 and 3 matter most for monthly payback.

One founder coming from ecommerce asked whether a €4.99 subscription could work with Meta ads, "or is it a trap at this stage?" The math above answers it: low prices can work, but only with a low enough cost per subscriber, a good annual mix, or strong retention.

## Read payback by channel

Payback differs a lot by channel and campaign. A channel with a higher cost per trial but better retention can pay back faster than a cheap one. Track cost per subscriber and retention for each channel, not just across the whole app.

## Payback period FAQ

### Is it bad if my cost per subscriber is higher than the first payment?

Not necessarily. For monthly plans, payback usually takes several months. It's only a problem if payback takes longer than your cash allows, or never happens because subscribers churn too fast.

### How do I calculate payback for a subscription app?

Divide cost per trial by trial-to-paid rate to get cost per subscriber. Then add up net revenue per original subscriber month by month, using your retention curve, until it exceeds that cost.

### Should I push annual or monthly plans?

Annual plans usually pay back faster because more revenue arrives up front. Test the plan mix on your paywall and compare payback and long-term retention.

### Do store fees change payback?

Yes. Always use net revenue after store fees. A 15% fee on a $7.99 plan means $6.79 per payment, which adds weeks to payback.

### What payback period is good for a subscription app?

It depends on your cash and growth goals. Many small teams aim to pay back within a few months; teams with funding may accept longer. Decide your limit first, then judge campaigns against it.

## The takeaway

A subscriber who costs more than their first payment isn't a loss if they keep paying. Calculate cost per subscriber, use net revenue, model retention, and judge each channel on whether it pays back in time.

## Why Your Ad Platform and Subscription Dashboard Never Match (and How to Reconcile Them)

URL: https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/ad-platform-vs-subscription-data-mismatch
Language: English
Published: 2026-11-04
Author: Luke

## Ad platform vs. subscription dashboard: why the numbers never match

You check your ad dashboard: 80 trial starts this week. You check your subscription dashboard: 55. Finance checks store payouts: different again. Many teams we talk to see the same gap and wonder which number to trust.

This is normal. Each tool is built to answer a different question, so each counts conversions differently.

## Six reasons the numbers differ

| Reason | Ad platform usually... | Subscription platform usually... |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1. Event definition | Counts the event you mapped, e.g. a trial start fired by your app | Counts store transactions, e.g. a trial that the store confirmed |
| 2. Date | Credits the conversion to the date of the ad click or view | Records the date the transaction happened |
| 3. Window | Counts conversions within its attribution window after a click or view | Has no attribution window; counts every transaction |
| 4. Privacy-protected data | May include modeled or aggregated conversions where user-level data isn't available | Counts only transactions it can see directly |
| 5. Other channels | Credits conversions it contributed to, even if another channel also did | Doesn't assign channels unless connected to an attribution tool |
| 6. Revenue | May show gross value you sent, in the currency you set | Shows proceeds after store fees, refunds and currency conversion |

  

[Six reasons ad platform and subscription dashboard numbers differ: event definition, date, attribution window, privacy-protected data, other channels and revenue]

### 1\. Event definition

Check exactly which event each tool counts. A trial start sent from your app the moment someone taps "Start trial" can fire before the store confirms it, or fire twice. Your subscription platform only counts the confirmed transaction.

### 2\. Date

Ad platforms usually credit a conversion to the day of the ad interaction. If someone clicks on Monday and starts a trial on Wednesday, the ad dashboard may show it on Monday, while your subscription dashboard shows it on Wednesday. Weekly totals shift between weeks.

### 3\. Attribution window

Each platform counts conversions within its own window after a click or view. Change the window and the count changes. A subscription dashboard has no window: it counts every transaction, whatever brought the user.

### 4\. Privacy-protected data

When user-level data isn't available, for example on iOS for people who don't allow tracking, ad platforms use privacy-preserving methods such as aggregated or modeled reporting. Those numbers are designed for campaign optimization and trend reading, so they won't line up user by user with transactions.

### 5\. Several channels claim the same user

A person might see a Meta ad, then a TikTok video, then search Apple Ads. Each platform may report that conversion in its own dashboard. Add up all your ad dashboards and you can easily count more conversions than your subscription platform has.

### 6\. Revenue values

Ad platforms show the value you sent with the event. Your subscription platform shows proceeds after store fees, refunds and currency conversion. The two will differ even when the event counts match.

## How to reconcile them

1.  **Pick a source of truth for each question.** Revenue and subscriber counts come from your subscription platform. "Which channel brought them" comes from one combined attribution view across channels. Each ad platform's own dashboard is best for optimizing inside that platform. If you use RevenueCat, see [how subscription and attribution tools fit together](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/do-i-need-an-mmp-with-revenuecat).
    
2.  **Align the event.** Make sure the trial start you send to ad platforms fires once per person, when the trial really begins.
    
3.  **Align dates and windows.** Compare the same date basis and the same attribution window, or compare by cohort (users acquired in week X) instead of by calendar day.
    
4.  **Compare ratios, not raw counts.** Track the ratio between the ad platform's trial count and your confirmed trials over time. A stable ratio means things are working. A sudden change means something broke, such as an event firing twice.
    
5.  **Deduplicate across channels.** Use one attribution tool that assigns each user to one source, so channels don't double-count.
    

## In summary

-   Ad platforms count conversions to optimize and report on their own campaigns. Subscription platforms count transactions to report revenue.
    
-   They differ in **what counts as a conversion, which date it's counted on, which window applies, how privacy-protected data is handled, and whether other channels also claim the same user**.
    
-   Don't look for one right number. Pick a source of truth for each question, align dates and windows, and compare ratios instead of raw counts.
    

## Questions we hear about mismatched numbers

### Why are my ad platform conversions higher than my subscription dashboard?

Usually because of attribution windows, conversions credited to the ad click date, modeled or aggregated conversions, events firing before the store confirms them, and several channels claiming the same user.

### Which number should I trust?

Use your subscription platform for revenue and subscriber counts, a combined attribution view to compare channels, and each ad platform's dashboard to optimize campaigns inside that platform.

### How big a difference is normal?

It depends on your setup, platforms and share of privacy-protected traffic. What matters more is whether the gap is stable over time. A sudden jump usually points to a tracking change or an event firing twice.

### How do I stop the same conversion being counted by several platforms?

Add them up only in a tool that assigns each user to one source. Each ad platform will still show its own view, which is fine for optimizing inside that platform.

### Should ad platforms and my subscription platform get the same events?

They should get the same definition of the event, sent once per person. That keeps optimization and reporting consistent, even if totals still differ.

## What to do next

Your ad dashboards and subscription dashboard aren't arguing. They're answering different questions. Decide which tool answers which question, align events, dates and windows, and watch the ratio between them instead of chasing one perfect number.

Author: Luke

## Apple Ads attribution starts in App Store search

Apple Ads puts your app at the top of App Store search results. Many people who see the ad tap it. Others scroll past, then find your app a few results down and install it anyway. Both groups arrive through App Store search.

  

[Apple Ads search results ad: an ad for an example travel app sits at the top of App Store search results for "vacation planner", with an organic result below it]

_Search results ad: the paid result is marked "Ad" and sits above the organic results for the same search. Source: Apple Ads_

  

[Apple Ads Search tab ad: an ad for an example app appears at the top of the Suggested list on the App Store Search tab, before anyone types a search]

_Search tab ad: Apple Ads can also show your app on the Search tab before someone types anything. Source: Apple Ads_

That makes a common question harder than it looks: how many of my installs, and how many of my subscribers, came from Apple Ads? One founder who looked into it explained why the reports don't simply add up: App Store Connect's search numbers include both organic and Apple Ads traffic, and the reports count different things, such as unique devices and page views on one side and impressions and taps on the other.

## Why App Store reports and Apple Ads reports measure different things

They're built for different jobs:

-   **App Store Connect analytics** shows how people find your product page and download your app, grouped by source type such as App Store search and App Store browse. It's designed to show your App Store presence as a whole.
    
-   **Apple Ads reporting** shows how your campaigns perform: impressions, taps, installs and cost by campaign, ad group and keyword.
    

Because the two use different units and views, subtracting one from the other gives a rough number at best. The cleaner approach is to tag the paid installs inside your own data.

## How to tag Apple Ads installs at the keyword level

Apple provides the [AdServices framework](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/adservices) for this. It works in four steps:

1.  Your app requests an **attribution token** from the AdServices framework on first launch.
    
2.  The framework generates the token.
    
3.  Your app or server sends the token to Apple's attribution API.
    
4.  The API returns an **attribution record** with campaign, ad group and keyword details when the install came from an Apple Ads campaign.
    

Store those fields with the user in your analytics or subscription platform. From then on, every trial start, purchase and renewal from that user can be grouped by campaign and keyword. Expect the Apple Ads dashboard and your subscription platform to show different numbers for the same campaign; here's [why ad platform and subscription numbers differ, and how to reconcile them](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/ad-platform-vs-subscription-data-mismatch).

Most MMPs and many subscription platforms can collect the token for you, so you don't have to build the server call yourself.

## Wire it up before you spend, not after

The attribution token is collected when a user first opens the app. If you add it after a campaign has run, you can't go back and tag those earlier installs.

One founder who wrote up his Apple Ads test put it plainly: "Take the time to wire up keyword attribution in your analytics before you run the campaign, not after."

A quick pre-launch checklist:

-   The attribution token is requested on first launch and sent to your analytics, MMP or subscription platform.
    
-   A test install from a campaign shows campaign and keyword fields in your data.
    
-   Trial start and purchase events are tracked for the same user.
    

## Read results by keyword: cost per trial, then cost per subscriber

Once installs are tagged, build a simple keyword table:

| Keyword | Spend | Installs | Trial starts | Cost per trial | Paid subscribers | Cost per subscriber |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Brand keyword | $120 | 150 | 60 | $2.00 | 24 | $5.00 |
| Category keyword | $400 | 260 | 52 | $7.69 | 15 | $26.67 |
| Competitor keyword | $300 | 120 | 12 | $25.00 | 3 | $100.00 |

_Numbers are illustrative._

  

[Apple Ads attribution example: cost per subscriber is $5.00 for a brand keyword, $26.67 for a category keyword and $100.00 for a competitor keyword (illustrative)]

A keyword with cheap installs can still be an expensive source of subscribers. Raise bids on keywords with low cost per subscriber, and lower or pause the ones that bring installs but few trials.

Two extra checks are worth doing:

-   **Brand keywords.** Brand campaigns keep your app at the top when people search your name. To see how much they add on top of organic, run a short, controlled test in one market and compare total trial starts.
    
-   **Country cohorts.** Trial-to-paid rates often differ by country. Read results per country before scaling a keyword everywhere.
    

## Key takeaways

-   Don't try to subtract Apple Ads from your App Store search numbers. The two reports measure different things.
    
-   Use the [Apple Ads Attribution API](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/adservices) to tag each install that came from an Apple Ads campaign, down to the ad group and keyword.
    
-   Follow those users to trial and subscription, and compare **cost per trial and cost per subscriber by keyword**.
    
-   Everything that isn't tagged is organic or another channel.
    

## Apple Ads attribution FAQ

### How do I tell Apple Ads installs apart from organic App Store installs?

Use the Apple Ads Attribution API. Your app requests an attribution token through the AdServices framework, and Apple returns campaign, ad group and keyword details for installs that came from Apple Ads. Untagged installs are organic or from other channels.

### Why don't App Store Connect and Apple Ads numbers match?

They answer different questions and count different things. App Store Connect reports your overall App Store presence by source, and Apple Ads reports campaign delivery such as impressions, taps and installs. Compare them as context, not line by line.

### Can I see which Apple Ads keywords bring paying subscribers?

Yes. Store the keyword from the attribution record with each user, then group their trial starts, purchases and renewals by keyword in your analytics, subscription platform or MMP.

### Do I need ATT consent for Apple Ads attribution?

Apple's attribution token is designed to work without the App Tracking Transparency prompt. Check Apple's current documentation for the exact data each response includes.

### Should I keep bidding on my brand keyword?

It depends on your market. Brand campaigns protect your name at the top of search results. To measure how much they add, run a short, controlled test in one market and compare total trial starts.

## Next steps

App Store search mixes paid and organic installs by design, so subtracting reports won't give you a clean answer. Tag Apple Ads installs with the attribution API, follow them to trial and subscription, and make bidding decisions on cost per subscriber by keyword.

## UGC Format Testing: How to Measure Formats Across Multiple Accounts

URL: https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/ugc-format-testing-multiple-accounts
Language: English
Published: 2026-11-04
Author: Luke

## UGC format testing across several accounts

More and more subscription apps run their own short-form accounts instead of, or alongside, paid creators. One founder planning this told us: "8-10 with different formats," adding that "most important is to find viral format first." A marketer who studies these formats made the same point from another angle: "what's more important is which format converts rather than what creator."

When you control the accounts, the account itself matters less. What you're really testing is the **format**: the hook, the structure, the way the app appears on screen.

**What this playbook sets up**

- Tag every post with its format, and give every account its own tracking link.

- Judge formats on **trials per 1,000 views** and **cost per trial**, not views.

- Kill a format after a fixed number of posts if it brings views but no trials.

- Double down on the format, not the account that happened to post it.

## Why views alone pick the wrong winners

Views tell you which format spreads. They don't tell you which format makes people install, start a trial and pay. Some formats are built to be shared: jokes, trends, reactions. Others are built to convert: a clear problem, the app solving it on screen, the app name said out loud.

One founder described how this played out in his own test: the format stayed constant and the conversion rate per format was "same across different videos/accounts so it just depended on views." That's the useful case. You only know it if you measure conversion per format, not just views.

## Step 1: Name your formats

Give each format a short, stable name and use it everywhere: in your post log, in link names and in reports. For example:

| Format       | Description                                                      |
|--------------|------------------------------------------------------------------|
| problem-demo | States a problem in the first 2 seconds, shows the app fixing it |
| before-after | Shows the result first, then how the app got there               |
| day-in-life  | The app appears naturally in a routine                           |
| list-tips    | "3 things I do every morning", with the app as one tip           |
| reaction     | Reacts to a trend or comment, app shown at the end               |

Keep the number of formats small, three to five at a time, so each one gets enough posts to judge.

## Step 2: One link per account, one tag per post

Give each account its own tracking link in the bio. Links in captions and comments aren't clickable on TikTok or Instagram, so the bio is where taps happen. Then log every post with its account, format, date and views.

If one account posts several formats, the link tells you which account a tap came from, and the post log tells you which format was live that day. Better still, dedicate each account to one format for a few weeks so link data maps straight to a format.

## Step 3: Add the signals links miss

Most viewers search the store instead of tapping a bio link, so links alone undercount every format. Add:

- **A one-tap onboarding question** listing your account names, so searchers can tell you where they saw you.

- **A trial-start read per day**, so you can see lift on days a format took off.

We explain how links, the survey and lift fit together in [Creator Attribution for Apps: How to Credit Installs When Viewers Skip the Link](https://www.airbridge.io/en/blog/creator-attribution-app-store-search).

## Step 4: Judge formats with two numbers

1.  **Trials per 1,000 views** = trials credited to the format ÷ views × 1,000. This tells you how well a format converts attention.

2.  **Cost per trial** = what you spent producing and posting the format ÷ trials credited to it. This tells you whether it pays.

Here is an illustrative month:

| Format       | Posts | Views   | Trials credited | Trials per 1,000 views |
|--------------|-------|---------|-----------------|------------------------|
| reaction     | 12    | 900,000 | 45              | 0.05                   |
| problem-demo | 12    | 240,000 | 96              | 0.40                   |
| before-after | 12    | 310,000 | 62              | 0.20                   |

*Numbers are illustrative.*

[UGC format testing example: reaction videos drew 900K views but 0.05 trials per 1,000 views, while problem-demo videos drew 240K views and 0.40 trials per 1,000 views (illustrative)]

The reaction format won on views and lost on everything else. The problem-demo format brought eight times as many trials per 1,000 views.

## Step 5: Set kill and scale rules before you start

Decide the rules up front, so you don't argue with yourself later:

- **Give each format at least 8 to 10 posts** before judging it. One post can flop or go viral by chance.

- **Kill a format** if trials per 1,000 views stay well below your average after that many posts.

- **Scale a format** by posting it on more accounts, not by keeping it on the account that found it.

- **Retest winners** every few weeks.

FAQ

Do I need to run paid ads to use Airbridge?

No. You can measure your posts, creators, and website too, not just ads.

If you do run ads, you can compare your organic and paid content side by side by installs, trials, and subscriptions.

Can I see which post or creator brought users?

Yes. Give each post or creator its own Airbridge Tracking Link. When people click it, you’ll see how many of them installed, started a trial, and subscribed.

One thing to know: if all your videos point to the same bio link, you’ll see results for that bio link as a whole, not for each video. And people who only watch, without clicking, can’t be tracked.

How UGC tracking works →
Can I track people who go from my website to my app?

Yes. Use an Airbridge Tracking Link anywhere you’d use a normal link on your site, like your download button or a banner. You’ll see who installed, started a trial, and subscribed.

The same link can send them straight to the right screen in your app, even if they install it first.

How web-to-app attribution works →
Do I need a developer to set it up?

You’ll need to install the Airbridge SDK in your app. It takes about an hour on average.

Building with Cursor, Claude Code, or Codex? Your AI agent can install it for you through Airbridge MCP.

Does Airbridge work with RevenueCat, Adapty, and Superwall?

Yes. Connect any of them to bring their subscription and paywall events into Airbridge, right next to the data on where your users came from.

You don’t need them, though. You can track those events with just the Airbridge SDK.

Airbridge Core Plan starts at $40 a month, with 500,000 data points included.

A data point is one event Airbridge collects for your app, like an install, a trial start, or a purchase. Clicks on your tracking links don’t count. Beyond 500,000, each extra data point is $0.0001.
